The susceptibility of facial recognition systems to fraudulent presentations restricts their adoption in high-stakes applications. Effective countermeasures against these deceptive attempts are vital for the safe integration of facial recognition technology. Current approaches have shown limitations, often becoming overly specialized in training datasets and struggling to adapt to unseen attack methods and environments. In this research, transfer learning is applied from the vision transformer model to tackle the challenge of detecting unknown anti-spoofing attacks. Experimental results conducted on widely accessible datasets showcase the superiority of our proposed solution, outperforming state-of-the-art methods significantly in zero-shot scenarios within the HQ-WMCA and SiW-M datasets, while also achieving substantial improvements in cross-database evaluations.

Deep reinforcement learning stands out as a promising AI paradigm for instructing machines via environmental interaction and adaptive learning from their errors. Despite initial expectations, however, its successful application in the automotive industry remains elusive. Following in the footsteps of notable achievements by Google DeepMind in mastering Atari games and Go, we have developed a comprehensive framework for autonomous driving through deep reinforcement learning, as detailed in our research publication. This framework leverages cutting-edge technology, incorporating multi-agent approaches such as PROPO and PROSAC, as well as a novel module based on the ShareNet design to facilitate the creation of policies with broad and inclusive knowledge. As a result, our framework has demonstrated impressive capabilities in navigating diverse and complex scenarios within the urban environment, as demonstrated by the successful completion of an urban race by the autonomous vehicle based on our model. This research breaks new ground in the advancement of deep reinforcement learning for autonomous driving, as a described in a recent paper approved for publication in the Journal of Intelligent Information Systems.

Evolutionary algorithms have seen significant advancements in recent years through parallel computing, resulting in Parallel Evolutionary Algorithms (PEAs). However, a major limitation in Asynchronous PEAs (APEAs) arises from idling computing nodes after each solution evaluation. As APEAs provide a higher chance of selection to quicker solutions, the evaluation time bias negatively affects the overall search performance. In an effort to address this drawback, a novel parent selection technique has been proposed to minimize the impact of evaluation time bias on APEAs. This innovative approach takes into account the frequency at which each solution is being evaluated and aims to ensure a uniform search progress across the population, disregarding the influence of evaluation time bias. Experiments conducted on multi-objective optimization problems have demonstrated the efficiency of the proposed paradigm. When compared to conventional parallelization methods, the results showed that the novel approach successfully reduced the evaluation time bias and subsequently improved the convergence rates of MOEA/D-DE. This, in turn, resulted in better quality solutions on specific test problems. Ultimately, the proposed paradigm overcame the drawback of asynchronous parallelization by addressing the evaluation time bias, unleashing the full potential of Asynchronous MOEA/DE in real-world settings.

The recent microlensing event OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 involved a cold super-Earth planet located among a group of eleven planets where the mass of the host stars ranges from hundreds to thousands of masses, leading to significant substructures in its light curve, making it challenging to determine the mass of the host star. By using the El~Chapo hint technique, we were able to precisely define the mass of the host star. Our research indicated that OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 has a mass of 0.76$+$/-0.13 M$_\odot$, placing the mass of its host star slightly above the critical value needed to see the gravitational effect of this planet using future Kepler-like telescopes. Additionally, our study obtained a more precise definition of the mass of the planet, 0.16$+$/-0.03 M$_\odot$, rather than 0.3 M$_\odot$. Using the gravitational microlensing effect, we were able to precisely calculate the mass of the host star of this planet and obtained a mass range of 0.76$+$/-0.13 to 0.36$+$/-0.08 M$_\odot) at a 95\% confidence interval. This new finding of a cold super-Earth makes OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 significantly notable and opens new pathways for astronomers to find cold super-Earth planets using the gravitational mic

The concept of an effective, time-independent Floquet Hamiltonian underpins the Floquet engineering of isolated systems, describing their evolution over driving periods and often obtained through analytical high-frequency expansions. However, extending these ideas to open quantum systems, modelled by a Markovian master equation of the Lindblad type, poses a significant challenge. In systems with only two energy levels, distinct phases arise where the Floquet generator may be either Markovian or not. Even within the high-frequency regime, numerical analysis sometimes reveals the existence of a Floquet Lindbladian generator but fails to reproduce this within analytical expansions. In a counterintuitive phenomenon, our study shows that, by choosing an appropriately rotating frame, a proper Floquet Lindbladian generator can be derived from high-frequency expansions, allowing us to describe a phase transition to lower driving frequencies. In the resulting phase, where the Floquet Lindbladian does not exist, we demonstrate that the generator's non-Markovian nature can be fully attributed to system-driven micromotion.

Our recent studies of the effects of Rh content in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ reveal the emergence of magnetic irreversibilities and spin freezing in the vicinity of x ≈ 0.6, accompanied by a suppression of long-range ferromagnetism. Through detailed analysis of the temperature and field histories, we observed pronounced evidence of long-range ferromagnetism below a specific Curie temperature for compositions containing x = 0.4, while compositions above x ≈ 0.6 displayed a spin freezing phenomenon in tiny ferromagnetic clusters at a characteristic freezing temperature. Upon performing zero-field cooling, followed by a heat treatment in the presence of an external field, the samples exhibited unique characteristics marked by a reversible shift in the temperature dependence of the neutron depolarization response between two freezing temperatures, thereby indicating a thermally-driven increase in the cluster size. These novel findings are substantiated by a microscopic description of the formation of a disordered magnetic phase, dubbed a Kondo-cluster glass, that coexists with a magnetic phase transition near the critical Rh content of x ≈ 0.6.

Using the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope, 19-beam tracking has successfully detected 19 individual 21 cm absorption lines toward the massive star-forming region G176.51+00.20. These absorption lines have narrow line widths of approximately 1.0 to 2.4 km/s, corresponding to ambient cloud temperatures of around 30 to 200 K. Following a routine search for self-absorption within the galactic rotation peaks, two regions of deep absorption have been found at galactic longitude values of approximately 9.950 and 9.980, displaying red and blue self-absorption features. This phenomenon is a result of one-sidedly embedded infrared dark clouds within the galactic molecular cloud. Furthermore, galactic rotation peak-like features have been detected in two other areas, displaying self-absorption at specific frequencies within the galactic rotation peaks, indicating the presence of galactic cloud fragments. This has led to the detection of 13 new absorption lines, increasing the total count to 32, which reveals a range of cloud kinetic temperatures of 6 to 21 km/s. This has significant implications for understanding the galactic cloud's structure and relationship with the massive star-forming region, as the detection of absorption lines at galactic rotation peaks offers a minimally biased method for identifying cloud fragments within the galactic molecular cloud. This has further implications for astronomers studying cloud fragmentation.

We demonstrate the topological equivalence of all intermediate beta-transformations with a specific type of transformation that removes a single non-repeating pattern from a greedy beta-transformation, known as an intermediate beta-shift with a hole. By employing an existing classification theorem for topologically intermediate transformations, it can be proved that such an intermediate beta-shift with a hole is topologically intermediate if and only if it exhibits a repeating pattern. As a result, we are able to classify the topological isomorphism types of all finite beta-transformations, finishing a classification first proposed by Block and Pearl.

Determining the CP-violating phase phi_s resulting from mixing-induced phenomena in Bs decays is a crucial method for discovering potential new physics phenomena. Utilizing approximately 7,421 +/- 105 signal events from predominantly CP-odd final states (J/\psi pi+ pi-), which were isolated in 1/fb of pp collision data gathered at a 7 TeV energy level by the LHCb detector, researchers performed a time-dependent analysis on the obtained data. As a result, phi_s was estimated to be -0.019 +/- 0.173 +/- 0.004 radians, in alignment with the Standard Model predictions. Furthermore, their findings revealed no indication of direct CP violation.

It is evident that deep neural networks excel in extracting relevant features from a given dataset, but they may not necessarily excel in adapting these features to datasets with different underlying characteristics. In this report, we compare the effectiveness of four domain adaptation methods for classifying images from the ResISC2 dataset, which requires recognizing earthquake damage levels. The non-linear classifications and diverse nature of the dataset make it a challenging task, and by employing the efficient Convolutional Neural Network architecture, known as MobileNet, we successfully achieve mean average precision of 71.16% for the original domain and 69.66% for multiple domains. Our experiments involving domain adaptation methods allow us to achieve improved results, with the original domain achieving a higher accuracy due to a more significant gap in data quality between the two domains, but we ultimately succeed in finding the best approach to adapt to the target domain.

In finite fields of dimension 2, an arc is a subset where no 3 points share a line. To determine the total number of such arcs, a specific counting method, called hypergraph containers, is employed to establish an upper bound on the total number of these arcs, represented as $\Omega(\frac{q^n}{n! log q})$. This containment approach in the paper also helps establish an asymptotic relationship for the total number of arcs in high-dimensional finite fields as the dimension approaches infinity.

A pictorial proof shows that there are $\binom{n+2}{4}$ equilateral triangles in a regular $n$-sided triangle by establishing a one-to-one correspondence between four-element subsets of the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n+2\}$ and the equilateral triangles in this grid, where it is visually represented by illustrating the triangle corresponding to the subset $\{4, 5, 8, 11\}$ when $n$ is $10$.

Despite recent advancements in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), explaining their predictive decisions remains an unresolved issue. Current methods primarily address the interpretation of individual cases (i.e., important graph structures and node attributes) to understand model predictions, but generate instance-specific explanations that fail to provide a broader understanding of the GNN model, restricting their general applicability in the inductive setting. Moreover, these methods struggle to provide natural explanations for groups of cases (e.g., graphs of the same class). To address these limitations, this study proposes a novel explainer for GNNs, PGExplainer, which parameterizes explanation generation using a deep neural network to explain groups of cases in an efficient and general manner. By adapting a Global Attention Mechanism and incorporating Spatial Embedding, PGExplainer outperformed existing state-of-the-art approaches on benchmark datasets, achieving up to a 2.71% accuracy improvement in our experiments.

The peculiar system, RXCJ0232.2-4420, at $z$ = 0.28, has an unusual system of radio sources located close to its center. To gain a deeper understanding of this complex system, we performed a detailed spatially-resolved radio analysis, alongside an X-ray spectral examination. Our findings indicate that the central radio sources are comprised of multiple distinct entities with different paths at the heart of this cluster. The leftmost radio source exhibits characteristics of a radio galaxy that has undergone interaction with the surrounding intracluster medium, as shown by its edge-wise drop in pressure and a decrease in temperature by a factor of two. On the other hand, the rightmost source appears to be active, with an unusually high temperature that surpasses that of the larger system by a factor of two. Our observations suggest that the central radio sources reside within filaments of gas that have been affected by past or on-going mergers within this cluster.

Recently, the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU), a novel type of recurrent neural network, was developed and has demonstrated superior performance on various benchmark datasets. In this work, the linear component of the LMU is optimized, resulting in a simplified variant that can be trained in parallel, thus overcoming the obstacle of GPU training limitations on RNNs. Our modification allows training to proceed up to 200 times faster. Furthermore, the performance of our model is evaluated on seven benchmarks in comparison to the original LMU and several other prominent deep networks. Our models consistently achieve superior results on these datasets and, in many cases, are parameter-efficient, achieving a new benchmark result on psMNIST and surpassing the performance of other state-of-the-art models, including DistilBERT and LSTMs on IMDB sentiment analysis.

As the next decade unfolds, the field of particle physics is driven by persistent questions about origin, primarily centered around why the universe has a matter predominance over antimatter, the universe's uniformity, and the enigma of dark matter. Solid astrophysical evidence points towards previously unexplored areas that may contribute to particle physics solutions. With its inherent properties, such as long-lived decay times or small coupling strengths, such particles are likely to require innovative experimental approaches that diverge from traditional techniques. This chapter discusses theory and measurement concepts for these particles, focusing on models including axion-like particles and dark photons that account for the dark matter phenomenon, along with states of dark matter potentially linked to baryon asymmetry and dark sectors affecting cosmology. Lastly, research on hidden sectors is explored as a means to a more unified theory of nature.

Language plays a vital role in a culture's fabric, deeply intertwined with human migration patterns. Investigating the migration dynamics through the naming game with migrating entities reveals how migration affects language development. (i) In scenarios where all agents are mobile, a collective movement emerges and variable experiments show that smaller groups tend to exhibit more uniform name distributions within their respective clusters. (ii) Conversely, when native speakers are stationary while the non-native speakers are mobile, the naming game tends toward coherence, meaning names converge to a single, shared value. Surprisingly, when both parties are free to move, coherent outcomes are less likely to occur. These findings demonstrate that coherent language achievement is more easily accomplished when the native and non-native speaker populations are physically separated by a barrier. By simulating the impact of a limited number of highly skilled language instructors, the results indicate that migration can facilitate global communication when names would naturally scatter without it. These conclusions not only provide a deeper understanding of the naming game with migrating entities but also shed new light on the intricate links between human migration and language evolution.

PINN algorithms have made significant breakthroughs in solving various complex PDE-based problems. Despite these achievements, they often struggle to achieve optimal convergence when the target function contains intricate details. By leveraging the properties of neural tangent kernels, we have investigated how PINNs with momentum affect their sample complexity. Our study reveals that incorporating momentum into PINNs significantly reduces the impact of spectral bias. As a result, we can observe improved convergence on problems with function embeddings of higher frequencies. Additionally, we examined the theoretical consequences of incorporating momentum during training and tested our hypotheses using variational inequality problems, which exhibit a universal spectral bias. Our experimental results confirm that using momentum consistently leads to increased network generalizability, as indicated by reduced overfitting and improved performance on out-of-distribution and noisy test data across multiple frequency settings.

We examine a two-wave system in the interval (-1,1), where one wave absorbs energy and the other does not, with partial damping that mimics a viscoelastic material's behavior. Prior research showed that with damping throughout the entire domain, the system's energy decreases at a rate proportional to $t^{-\frac{1}{2}}$. Using the frequency domain method in this paper, we demonstrate the system's behavior changes significantly due to the waves being coupled and the non-smooth damping term, specifically that it loses its rapid exponential stability and instead experiences a slowing decay at a rate no better than $t^{-\frac{1}{12}}$.

Highly-constrained environments pose a significant challenge for traditional machine learning methods, primarily because self-supervised data collection is too costly, risking financial losses and causing data biases that exacerbate the problem.  Reinforcement learning successes in games and robotics offer incentives for improved performance, but the need for vast amounts of interaction with the environment, along with inadequate data safety mechanisms, creates risks of system failures and accidents.  Consequently, there's an increasing desire to harness the power of knowledge at the human level to inform decision-making, particularly through knowledge-based reinforcement learning.  KBRL algorithms absorb insights from experts through a semi-supervised format, combining voluminous action suggestions with concise, high-value feedback.  This enables the efficient learning within complex environments characteristic of industrial tasks such as intricate assembly processes.  However, current KBRL methods primarily focus on optimizing the model's efficiency, leaving the development of explainable and interpretable strategies unaddressed.  To bridge this gap, researchers propose a novel three-layered hierarchical framework built on rules extracted via inductive logic programming.  First, the initial framework aggregates related action suggestions into compact, high-level commands with predictive signatures, facilitating data efficiency through centralized representations.  Next, the second layer leverages the signature predictions to generate abstract state representations with predictive significance, enabling the downscaling of the observational space while preserving the richness of the task environment.  Finally, the proposed third layer efficiently learns action predictions using the generated symbolic state representations, enabling the learning of

We've developed an all-optical technique for producing optical nonreciprocity on a microchip, achieved through the process of quantum squeezing a specific mode in coupled resonator systems. A key factor in this method involves applying classical coherent light in a one-way fashion to parametrically pump a nonlinear resonator. The quantum fluctuation amplification in this resonator forces adjacent cavity modes to become entangled, causing them to exhibit imbalanced photon statistics upon measurement. This property enables the setup to act as a nonreciprocal gate for light by allowing us to implement a directional gate for quantum information. Notably, when used in conjunction with a single photon source, the technique enables us to perform'measure and reconstruct' methods to restore and map out a quantum mechanical field that would otherwise be inaccessible.

We expand upon the minimax problem first studied by Fenton by considering functions of the form $f(x-h)$ with $h\in\mathbb{Z}$, where $f$ is a real-valued function, and investigating the configuration $(M, d)$ with $M = \{[n, n+1): n\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ and $d$ being the standard metric on $\mathbb{R}$. Our work involves developing Fenton type theorems for this setting, including a relative of the Fenton Lemma, to determine when a configuration can be Carathéodory-regular, and identifying unique normalization conditions that must be met for $F(x-h)$ to be Carathéodory-regular. Additionally, we establish a connection between this problem's solvability and the van der Monde determinant given specific values for $f(0)$, $f(1)$, and $p\in\mathbb{R}$, revealing a connection that can be utilized to solve a pointwise version of the problem.

The CRESST experiment is one of the leading projects for directly detecting dark matter particles weighing less than GeV/c$^2$. Its ability to analyze numerous isotopes within its target material is an advantage in exploring dark matter interactions. This research focuses on dark matter interactions with $^{6}$Li nuclei, one of the least studied targets in CRESST. By calculating interactions with dark matter particles having a mass equal to that of $^{6}$Li and featuring interactions with nucleons as well as vector and axial vectors, it is determined that experimental results can be utilized to separate favorable and disfavorable interactions between dark matter particles and $^{6}$Li nuclei.

Blind Image deblurring attempts to estimate a latent image's sharpness and a blurred image, an ill-posed problem, resolved by restricting either the image or a blur kernel representing blur. Differing from prior research, this study regulates the structure of the blur kernel. The kernel mixture concept utilizes Gaussian kernels with enhanced scale and center configurations, producing a nearly non-parametric blur shape representation. The decision of the base kernel count becomes more flexible due to a data-driven method. This strategy is applied to popular deblurring algorithms, including SHAKE and Lissage, and significantly yields superior results with improved flexibility in the number of base kernels. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/diegoVitkin/Blind-Deblurring-Kernel-Mixture.

This paper introduces a new concept called associative BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair with weight (λ,γ) which can be used to solve the double curved Rota-Baxter BiHom-system. Furthermore, we establish equivalent definitions of covariant BiHom-bialgebra with quasitriangular properties and show that its BiHom-one-parameter group of Rota-Baxter algebras can be formed from the associative BiHom-Yang-Baxter equation solution set. Additionally, this paper proves that the BiHom-Yang-Baxter equation has two equivalent concordant forms that arise from the associative variant and provides a representative example.

Formal verification offers critical correctness assurances for software,
particularly vital in systems requiring safety and security assurances.
Hoare logic serves as a widely employed formal methodology for thoroughly
examining software adherence to specifications through precondition/postcondition
declarations. The improvement of semantic parsing methods and increasing
computational capabilities enable processing large amounts of natural language
input, making it feasible to extract logical forms (i.e., meaning representations)
from natural language inputs and utilize them as pre/post-conditions in Hoare
logic. This study presents an approach to formally verifying software based on
previously established programs and natural language specifications through
Hoare logic applications. The research employs the HOL framework but suggests a more
practical yet straightforward finite state machine verification method due to
HOL's conceptual and implementation difficulties. The paper demonstrates the proposed
method's feasibility using the practicality of verifying a stack-based push-down
system through Hoare logic, even without employing HOL. Ultimately, the goal is to
develop a general framework for this purpose.

Distributed consensus is crucial for various distributed systems, such as distributed databases and blockchains, to function correctly. The Canopus protocol efficiently manages large-scale distributed consensus without the need for a single leader, achieving this through a virtual tree structure that limits network traffic and hardware redundancies within the network. The existing Canopus protocol excels at scalability but falls short when dealing with failures and malicious attacks. To address this limitation, this paper presents RCanopus, an improved protocol that enhances Canopus's failure handling and fault tolerance by introducing two key features: redundant consensus filtering, which prevents an attacker from blocking consensus by disrupting the network; and system-wide failure resiliency, which allows the system to continue operating even in the presence of multiple failures or attacks. The performance of RCanopus is evaluated and compared to other protocols, with impressive results that show it can achieve high-performance consensus with failure resiliency and minimal overhead.

Recent studies utilizing neutron spin echo and nuclear magnetic resonance relaxation methods, which examine linear transport properties, have yielded contrasting results when analyzing the impact of cholesterol on the bending modulus of lipid bilayers. This inconsistency arose despite earlier research employing solely equilibrium experiments, not linear transport properties, indicating that one may be misled by data from the latter. A general discussion highlights how this misunderstanding occurs, after which it's demonstrated that the neutron spin echo findings can be reinterpreted to be consistent with the prior equilibrium results, thereby resolving the disparity. Furthermore, in the context of nuclear magnetic resonance relaxation methods, there exists a degree of uncertainty which could also reconcile the differences.

This paper examines the loop quantum cosmological model generated from the ADM Hamiltonian. It looks at a spatially homogeneous, flat FRW model and finds that its modified Friedmann equation is analogous to that of the APS LQC model. Notably, the model's critical matter density at the bounce point is a quarter of the original APS LQC model's, with the critical density $\rho_{cL}$ equalling $\frac{\rho_c}{4}$. This discovery implies that quantum gravity effects will manifest earlier than previously thought and also make detection potentially easier due to a lower critical density.

The Pierre Auger Observatory catalog details 100 extensive air-showers 
recorded between 2004 and 2020 for high-energy particles, spanning a specific
energy range from 78 to 166 EeV. This comprehensive dataset is made available 
for close examination, alongside nine events used to establish the energy scale 
for each detected primary particle. An accompanying plot displays the locations 
where these energetic particles entered Earth's atmosphere, leaving their data unanalyzed.

Incorporating deep neural networks into robotic systems poses a significant problem due to the lack of reliable measures for their output predictions. Researchers have developed uncertainty estimation methods for deep object detectors but encountered difficulties with information loss during non-maximum suppression and the multitasking nature of detectors. A novel approach using Bayesian inference has been proposed to overcome these challenges by designing a decoder network that simultaneously estimates class and bounding box uncertainties. The method has been further enhanced with adaptive non-maximum suppression, taking into account the uncertainty levels to improve accuracy. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in uncertainty estimation and achieves consistent improvements in uncertainty assessment for real-world scenarios on widely used object recognition datasets (VOCS-2007, VOCS-2012, PASCAL-VOC). The associated code and model weights can be accessed through the DeepROX platform at a specified location.

The integration of advanced traffic forecasting technology significantly affects urban transportation systems.
The traffic4cast competition, held during ICAIS 2019, aimed to enhance traffic prediction accuracy by leveraging real-time traffic data from cities. Two related sub-competitions focused on short-term traffic forecasting for specific locations in Skopje, North Macedonia. The first sub-competition required predicting total vehicle flow rather than individual vehicle positions. The second sub-competition involved predicting vehicle position distribution within a given area. The competition's first part drew substantial international participation, yielding 71 solution submissions. The second part also garnered interest, with 28 submitted solutions. The provided data included historical traffic information, but as an untested assumption, no information about past vehicle locations or speeds was available. Participants predicted vehicle positions based on first-in-first-out principle and total vehicle flow based on pixel analysis. Notably, participants from China dominated both sub-competitions. Pre-trained models, specifically GANs and Dilated Convolutional Network, also exhibited superior performance. The article discusses participating strategies, summarizes performance, analyzes results, and identifies areas for improvement.

We have developed a rewriting system within the realm of Gray categories, which will be utilized to prove coherence for the strict higher groupoids. This rewriting system has been extended into bialgebraic Gray categories, allowing for the derivation of coherence results for braided and bi-brated higher categories. These coherence results can be seen as a combination of earlier research by Klisovyi, Valentinov, and Parker. Moreover, our methodology has been adapted to the category of strict higher categories, yielding coherence results for certain diagrammatic and monadic structures. This study is published as a chapter within the edited book 'Diagrammatic Mackey Theory and Representations of Brouwerian Groups', which is set to be published.

Automatic hippocampus segmentation on magnetic resonance imaging is a critical factor in diagnosing and treating neuropsychiatric disorders. Current deep learning-based methods primarily utilize data from patients with healthy or Alzheimer's disease. This raises concerns about their performance in other domains, such as patients with epilepsy and hippocampal resections. We have developed and validated an open-source, state-of-the-art deep learning method that uses an extended 2D multi-orientation approach with automatic pre-processing and orientation alignment. We compared this method with other recent deep learning techniques in two datasets: the public HarP dataset and an in-house epilepsy dataset, HCUnicamp. Despite surpassing other methods in terms of Dice coefficient, our approach as well as other tested methods failed to completely avoid false positives in resection regions when applied to epilepsy patients, indicating room for further improvement.

We scrutinize an experiment claiming to showcase the quantum pigeonhole effect by having three parties navigate a two-path interferometer with no pair of them using the same path simultaneously. Through an analysis based on weak values, we uncover inconsistencies in the description. By incorporating transversal modes and examining the emergence of correlations between path and traversal properties, we also investigate the rotational symmetry of the output pattern as an alternative indicator of three-body correlation. However, our analysis finds that the symmetry cannot be attributed to a three-body effect, rather it's a consequence of two-body correlation due to two particles simultaneously exiting the interferometer, leading to the apparent triangular pattern. Moreover, our work illustrates how weak-value measurements can facilitate the detection of two-body correlations in this setup.

Our research identifies the Cosmic Ray Albedo Neutron Decay (CRAND) as the primary factor responsible for the formation of high-energy inner proton radiation belts. A Monte Carlo simulation model is created to simulate and analyze proton radiation generated by decaying neutrons in the atmosphere, trapped in the Low Earth Orbit (LEO) region. The model's primary outcomes include the spatial and energy distributions of trapped protons at low altitudes, as well as the variations in count rates and energy spectra of protons detected by a Silicon Detector on board a satellite. By comparing our simulation results to actual measurement data of protons detected by the SiD detector on the Edge of Space mission, we are able to quantify the CRAND effect on proton radiation in LEO.

A network's expressivity is a crucial factor in assessing deep neural networks, 
as it correlates directly with the limitations of achievable performance gains. This 
paper proposes a novel three-phase training approach based on expressivity 
criteria, consisting of global model reduction, weight refinement, and architecture 
redesign. The first phase reduces networks by iteratively applying model 
generalization and selecting key neurons through gap-sensitive pruning, 
utilizing a novel neural gap estimator. The second stage refines weights through 
a generated proxy model, as well as adversarial data, to enforce label 
consistency. Ultimately, the paper presents an in-depth analysis of GNN 
architecture design, incorporating structural, spatial, and temporal 
considerations, and applies VAE and GAN training to enhance GNN representation 
and robustness. Empirical evidence across multiple visual tasks and datasets 
validates the proposed training method's superior performance, as well as the 
corresponding state-of-the-art GNN architectures.

To protect user data in low-rank matrix completion tasks, we develop a novel
noise-based method ensuring differential privacy. This method incorporates
noise with characteristics inspired by the Huber loss function in robust
statistics, and is termed as the Huber mechanism. In our study, we evaluate the
performance of this huber mechanism against other privacy mechanisms, including
using the alternating least squares iteration method from numerical experiments.
Furthermore, we demonstrate the sensitivity of the huber mechanism and its
ability to maintain differential privacy using the Poisson perturbation method.
Ultimately, we compare the effectiveness of different mechanisms in estimating
missing matrix entries with different types of noise.

We propose a novel approach to modelling interstellar dust where larger grains are comprised of a uniform material, referred to as 'astrodust', and tiny particles, known as PAHs, come in various distinct forms. Our analysis of the Riemann sink in the astrodust component reveals that it should be implemented as a Riemann sum instead of a continuous process, and this insight inspires an improved algorithm for pahs. By using data from various observational studies, we determine that the size distribution of carbon grains conforms to an accurate mathematical distribution, and our research suggests that carbon and silicate grains have differing optical properties. PAHs, on the basis of their observed polarization properties, are predicted to have a relatively small size range with diameters less than $1.0nm$. Our model accurately reproduces the overall slope of the 217nm absorption feature and accounts for its complexity, and this pattern originates primarily from smaller carbon grains. Our research indicates that larger grains are primarily responsible for the overall slope and/or curvature of the extinction law and not the lesser and highly aligned PAHs. Our model accounts for grain alignment and optical properties which are controlled by magnetic fields. By using data from the Hershel Infrared Spectrometer and the Composite Spectroscopic Law, we can accurately simulate the FIR emission and the overall slope and/or curvature of the extinction law and/or polarization curves. Our model effectively predicts the relative amounts of different interstellar substances.

Research on exoplanets has led to groundbreaking discoveries surrounding low-mass stars, like those at TRAPPIST-1 and Proxima Centauri, but theoretical models fail to account for the formation of giant planets in such environments. Recent high-resolution ALMA observations of CIDA 1, a Taurus low-mass star, show disk substructures indicative of a massive planet. Our aim is to simulate CIDA 1's dust ring using ALMA Band 7 and 4, as well as $^{12}$CO and $^{13}$CO channel maps, assuming it's formed from a planet interaction. We utilized the PIONIER and VLTI/differential speckle interferometry to further investigate this matter. Our model reveals that the observed dust ring is predominantly composed of millimeter and submillimeter grains with a similar spatial distribution, but with distinct scales and gas reservoirs. Using sensitive MUSE data and VLTI/diffuser, we detected no signs of a planet, however its presence could have escaped our detection. Our calculations indicate that the mass of the putative planet is substantial, around 1-3 Jupiter masses, and support the model suggesting its epicylic origin. Moreover, mass loss through the disk may prevent gas giant formation around low-mass stars due to the protrusion of the orbiting planet into the surrounding disk. Early detection of such planets is critical, as they may lead to gas dissipation, as seen in CIDA 1

Consider the rules of a popular light-switching game played on a simple graph with vertices of clickable lights. Each click affects the state of the chosen light and its neighboring lights. A sequence of strategic clicks leads to winning, which means turning off all lights in a predetermined arrangement. Inspired by the original Lights Out game from Tiger Electronics, we're investigating an extension known as the Most Clicks Problem, a combinatorial optimization challenge where the goal is to develop the most effective click sequence to turn off all lights on a given graph. A thorough examination of this problem involves examining various approaches and upper limits for solving them efficiently.

This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, combining the techniques of image restoration and image segmentation. The integration of image restoration aspects enables the proposed method to effectively handle images corrupted by noise, blurriness, missing pixels, and varied color schemes. Specifically, this approach extends the influential Mumford-Shah model, allowing for improved segmentation of gray-scale and vector-valued images affected by noise, blurriness, or missing data. Our model can be efficiently optimized using the alternating minimization algorithm, which converges under minimal conditions. Our proposed method achieves superior performance in experiments, compared to existing state-of-the-art segmentation models.

Program analysis through Abstract Interpretation involves simulating the behavior of a program in a simplified environment to approximate its true behavior. This simulation has two distinct phases, consisting of the initial creation of a abstract representation of the program and its subsequent analysis. These phases can be viewed as representing the program's construction and its subsequent flow. These phases are typically carried out consecutively, though they could be joined into a single pass on a domain that accurately conveys both the program's past and current states. This paper proposes a method to distinguish between the phases in analysis by utilising a domain that incorporates both past and current information that is based on a domain that accurately conveys both, such as the Subdirect product of convex sets in a complete lattice.

A broad range of structural phases in perovskite oxides host various physical properties that contribute to a variety of technological applications. Topological phonons, encompassing nodal rings, lines, and points, are found in different oxide perovskite systems, encompassing structural forms (tetragonal, orthorhombic, rhombohedral), compounds (BaTiO3, PbTiO3, SrTiO3), and external influences (photoexcitation, strain, temperature). Notably, tetragonal perovskite compounds stabilized through photoexcitation exhibit all topological phonon types simultaneously, whereas thermal stabilization primarily supports a limited set of topological phonon states. Furthermore, we demonstrate the potential to regulate topological phonon states through photoinduced carrier concentrations without accompanying structural transformations, suggesting that light manipulation may lead to transitions between states without altering the phase of the system. We propose perovskite oxides as a versatile experimental platform to investigate topological phonons and manipulate them with the aid of light.

Unsupervised outlier detection in various fields such as data mining and machine learning relies heavily on distance-based methods due to their adaptability in generic metric spaces. Research has been focused on improving outlier detection by enhancing the capability to identify nearest neighbors quickly, typically utilizing graph structures in this process. However, the outcome often results in subpar precision or performance issues due to oversimplification or limitations in handling complex distances. To overcome these challenges, a novel graph-based method is proposed, grounded in a theorem that allows for the development of an adaptable nearest neighbor search algorithm, precision of which is proven through theoretical analysis. By applying this concept, a dynamic graph can efficiently detect outliers in the order of n logn and for clustering in the order of n logn. Experimental verification confirms the proposed method excels over existing methods across diverse data sets, demonstrating superior precision and performance.

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a stationary, perfectly conducting plane. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied on the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated versus an atom at rest encountering a moving mirror.

As applications relying on graph representations grow, the focus has shifted from global fairness to incorporating fairness at the node level, considering that Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based models primarily operate within local neighborhoods. To address this gap, we propose a framework that captures the concept of neighborhood fairness. Our method is built on two core components - the first enables the construction of equitable neighborhoods for any node in a graph and the second allows integration of these equitable neighborhoods into comprehensive graph structures. Notably, while existing studies have suggested linking nodes based on structural similarities, our approach differs in that it considers the equitable property as a key attribute for connecting nodes. Through comprehensive experiments, we demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches in terms of both model and graph quality.

This research focuses on kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions and evaluates the effectiveness of two analytical techniques in obtaining approximate solutions to these models. We apply and compare the Homotopy Perturbation Method and the Simple Iteration Method to derive approximate analytical solutions to non-linear equations describing reversible enzyme reactions.  The resulting approximations demonstrate a comparable level of accuracy.  Supporting Matlab codes for both methods are provided in the appendices.

Theoretical physicists conduct experiments in final stages with data obtained from proton-proton collisions, utilizing the CMS detector at CERN. In a 2016 study with 35.9 inverse femtobarns of recorded data and 13 TeV of centre-of-mass energy, researchers searched for evidence of supersymmetry in final stages characterized by the presence of the neutrino and at least one large-jet. In the course of the analysis, the points with predicted frequencies were determined across a range of 300-3000 GeV for masses of gluino, and up to 1200 and 2400 GeV for masses of top squark with single and double production respectively. The study's findings exclude the possibility of the gluino with predicted frequencies at least in four sigma from the frequency spectrum of the standard model, across a range of 300-3000 GeV for masses of gluino. Moreover, the study's findings exclude the possibility of the top squark with predicted frequencies at least in four sigma from the frequency spectrum of the standard model, across a range of 675-3000 GeV for masses of 1100-1200 GeV for models including or excluding the effects of the Higgs boson respectively.

Two proposed tests for identifying rational expectations financial bubbles with predictable endpoints are presented and validated using Monte Carlo simulations. These tests can detect bubbles even when crash times are influenced by external factors not accounted for in current models. The first test incorporates an additional factor considering the expected duration of bubbles. The second test enhances the first by utilizing an expected expiration date. The efficiency of these tests is compared using various scenarios, including different bubble patterns, anticipation lengths, and distribution types governing the end times. The results show that incorporating the expected expiration date into the model significantly enhances the accuracy of bubble detection. Furthermore, it's observed that the expected expiration date can effectively replicate the performance of the optimal bubble termination date for a wide range of parameter values, which can be calculated through numerical methods not involving market data. The study also examines the robustness of these tests by introducing noise into the model and finds that the presence of noise slightly decreases the power of the tests. Consequently, the proposed tests offer valuable tools for identifying rational expectations financial bubbles that are scheduled to terminate at a specific point in time.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to compute theoretical predictions, and a global overdamped dynamics approach via the Euler method was used to generate random dynamics trajectories for the final simulations. Notably, the S matrix method, which directly evaluates an integral with a constant determinant, performed better than the Zuber-Feldman matrix method, which involves a more complex transformation and higher dimensional integrals. Moreover, the S matrix method's acceptance rate issues did not impact the precision of our final results as they did the Zuber-Feldman method's. Trajectory-based simulations, which involve evaluating an exponential of an integral with constant properties, performed even better still.

Recent research has shown significant progress in improving recommender system performance through leveraging reviews for predicting ratings, however the current methods have several limitations. The existing techniques often use complex neural networks, which make it challenging to easily understand reviewer sentiments. Moreover, they tend to overlook the unique interaction between reviews and users/items, where each review contributes differently to modeling user/item preferences. To overcome these challenges, a new approach called Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN) has been proposed for review-based item recommendations. The method starts by encoding user/item reviews using BERT and introduces a lightweight sentiment extractor to capture review semantics. A sentiment prediction task guides this sentiment extractor to identify relevant features. A rating prediction task then follows, which integrates a rating learner with an interactive module that combines identity and review representations to allow interactive features to collectively influence the final rating score. Experimental results on several real-world datasets show that the proposed model surpasses the current state-of-the-art models.

Developing CS NLP systems is obstructed by the scarcity of CS data. This study delves into utilizing data augmentation methods to create Dialectal Arabic-English CS text, by replacing words with alternative dialects, to boost the performance of CS NLP systems. The investigation includes various data augmentation techniques on short and long CS text sequences, evaluating their impact on Arabic and English individual words and CS wordswitched context. The analysis covers a range of NLP tasks from morphological analysis to machine translation in both dialects, revealing that basic word replacement outperforms other data augmentation methods across the board. Interestingly, it is observed that using short CS text is beneficial for enhancing CS NLP system performance. Moreover, it is found that utilizing a dictionary-based tool instead of an LE dictionary yields better results. The findings provide valuable insights for future research on CS data augmentation.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure.

We're investigating integrable boundary conditions that can be geometrically interpreted as D-branes within specific theoretical models based on products of group- and coset-spaces, which are generalized versions of lambda deformations. Utilizing a sigma-model approach, we found all the boundary conditions that maintain the model's integrability, and discovered that they can be described by conformal branes in the un-deformed state, whose properties are known in detail. Our work generalizes previous findings on the integrability of boundary states in the classical context and the underlying geometric symmetries. It also yields new insights for the basic setup.

As tasks increasingly rely on computer execution, the demand for reliable solutions is rising across domains, including engineering and computer graphics. A crucial requirement for domain-specific applications is mesh manipulation, which involves a category of problems known as constraint-based system optimization. These optimization problems, characterized by constraints limiting a set of variables and objectives that need to be maximized or minimized, are encountered in tasks such as maintaining a consistent mesh layout. To address this requirement, researchers have developed an efficient algorithm for untangling hexahedral meshes in order to minimize the cost of complex operations like complex trigonometric multiprime decompositions. This algorithm has been successfully applied to large meshes, allowing rapid identification of tangled elements with a linear complexity of O(n), where n represents the number of vertices. A graphical representation of the untangled mesh topology is provided through a color scheme that quickly identifies tangled regions, in addition to a vertex color coding system to visualize distance metrics between vertices. Although primarily developed for optimization problems in mesh manipulation, this algorithm can also solve up to 58 tetrahedralization problems with a high success rate, making it a versatile tool.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their core mechanisms, which allows them to complement each other
effectively. To prove this, we've developed a simple approach where relation
extraction models are enhanced by incorporating techniques commonly used in
knowledge graph link prediction. To do this, we've employed a joint training
paradigm that simulates unknown knowledge graph links, utilizing a knowledge
graph benchmark to assess its impact. Our findings demonstrate that this
paradigm not only helps in identifying unknown relation extraction scenarios
but also increases the overall extraction accuracy by improving model general
adaptability. We've conducted thorough experiments on five standard benchmarks
(ConceptNet, TACKBERT, CheQA, CheRIA, and SciIE) that cover various domains,
which substantiate our claims with empirical evidence.

This study introduces an innovative analytical delay model specifically tailored for deep submicron CMOS inverters. Developed based on the critical recognition that inverter delay is influenced by multiple process variables and load capacitance, the proposed model incorporates the effects of channel length, power supply voltage, and output load capacitance. Unlike conventional models, this delay model considers the nonlinear relationship between transition time and load capacitance. To derive the transition time formula, the proposed model utilizes the user-friendly Curve Fitting Toolbox in Matlab, eliminating the need for iterative trial and error in determining fitting parameters. To validate the accuracy of the proposed model, the analytical delay was compared with SPICE simulations for a wide range of technological parameters. The results demonstrate the proposed model's high precision, with absolute error percentages peaking at 10.05% and averaging around 4.15%. The proposed model is in the form that can be used for quick design purposes.

Making optimal decisions in complex, continuously changing environments requires
assuming certain conditions. Often, researchers assume a certain level of consistency
in the decision-making model known as the Q-function. However, in numerous real-world scenarios,
this condition does not hold true. Instead, we propose a more adaptable way of measuring the consistency of Q-functions
in various complex environments. This new approach enables us to establish tighter limits on our model's behavior, resulting
in improved learning efficiency. Additionally, we provide a theoretical understanding of our approach and discuss its potential applications in continuous decision-making processes.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. When combined, they fully captured the continuum, and our data indicated distinct posterior regions associated with each. The results of this study demonstrate the complex nature of the animacy spectrum in VTC, revealing it to be composed of multiple interconnected spectral dimensions.

In scientific simulation, achieving accurate replication of real-world scenarios is a top priority. However, commonly used methods such as the finite element method and finite volume method are often prone to inaccuracies and artifacts, like Gibbs oscillations, particularly when approximating complex characteristics. This necessitates an efficient and accurate approach that can effectively remove inaccuracies and enhance the overall quality of the solution. Our research focuses on convex optimization-based filters that preserve the well Posedness and stability of the original partial differential equations. These filters draw inspiration from the work of Chiyne and Garabnik, and have been successfully applied in one-dimensional spaces with proven results. This study aims to extend this application to higher dimensional spaces by combining the Barycentric Interpolation with a one-dimensional filter on each dimension, and utilizing the Schwarz Alternating Method to merge the filtered outcomes from each dimension. The proposed algorithm was tested on 2D and 3D cases, demonstrating its ability to preserve the continuous field nature and maintain the stability of the numerical solution while accurately approximating the original data. This method has the further benefit of allowing for an adjustment of the filter's influence on space and time parameters through the management of the convex optimization problem's coefficients.

Quasi-periodic oscillations type C, typically observed in low-hard and hard-intermediate states of black hole X-ray transients, have been investigated using the MAXI J1535-571 data collected by Insight-HXMT. By applying a novel time-dependent Comptonization model and a relativistic reflection model, researchers have demonstrated its ability to accurately describe X-ray data up to 100 keV in the hard-intermediate state. Observations show the type C QPO frequency varied between 2.1 to 3.3 Hz, and then sharply increased to ~9 Hz. This phenomenon is associated with the evolution of corona size and feedback fraction. When correlated with radio observations, these findings suggest that the morphology of the corona might influence the accretion disk size and shape, ultimately driving coronae formation and structure change in a strategy-oriented strategy, namely, the accretion disk-truncated model.

In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly for tasks requiring cooperation and communication, MARL agents are prone to being brittle due to their potential for overfitting on the policies of their training partners. As a result, they may adapt strategies centered on preconceived expectations of other agents' actions rather than truly reacting to their behaviors. To address this issue, we developed transfer empowerment as a method that quantifies the influence between the actions of individual agents and aims to guide MARL agents toward developing reactive approaches. Three simulated cooperation scenarios confirm our hypothesis that this approach leads to improved performance in multi-agent settings, making transfer empowerment a promising principle for enhancing the effectiveness of MARL coordination through increased reactivity to partner behaviors.

We introduce MatSim, a comprehensive synthetic dataset, benchmark, and 
approach designed to leverage computer vision for identifying and 
transferring properties of visual materials. By leveraging physics-based 
rendering, we generate a wide array of realistic material appearances, 
allowing us to train a model that can identify materials across diverse 
scenes and views. Our novel CLPR framework harnesses contrastive learning 
while utilizing physics-based rendering to develop a material embedding. 
This representation facilitates one-shot classification of materials 
regardless of perspective or environment. Moreover, we successfully 
demonstrate the applicability of our framework to extricating material 
properties from real-world images.

Two equivalent formulations of Lie 2-algebras are recalled: one as a categorification of Lie algebras and another as 2-term L∞-algebras. The paper proceeds by introducing four different types of Lie 2-algebras derived from categorifying simple Lie algebras, using examples from U2(2) and SU2 to illustrate the concept. Furthermore, the integration of Lie 2-algebras into the realm of Lie 2-groups is discussed, with an emphasis on constructing 2-groups from the Lie 2-algebras previously defined, utilizing two distinct methods: one involving smooth functors between 2-categories and another based on homotopy types. The paper is completed by a discussion of the field of Lie 2-algebras and Lie 2-groups as a rapidly evolving area of research.

We introduce a novel method for local image feature matching, where instead of a sequential process, we first identify pixel-wise dense matches at a basic level and then refine the good matches at a detailed level. In contrast to other dense methods, we innovatively employ self and cross attention mechanisms in transformers to accurately match pixels within and between images. This approach eliminates the need for expensive hardware accelerations like GPUs and IGZ for high-quality results. Experimental outcomes confirm that our method, called LoFTR, surpasses other dense and detector-based techniques and can be combined with robust features to yield exceptional performance. Moreover, our result showcases the significant potential of transformer-based features in computer vision. The LoFTR method is freely available at https://github.com/acmtu/LoFTR.

The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue has been identified previously; however, the current study aims to provide a more in-depth analysis, including an exploration of its causes. It appears that noisy data and the employement of an ill-posed inverse problem are primary contributing factors, although the specific mechanisms underlying their impact are not fully understood. To address these issues, the paper recommends two key approaches. Firstly, the utilization of polarimetric flux maps to enhance the signal-to-noise ratio and facilitate stability in the inverse problem. Secondly, the incorporation of regularization techniques to reduce the ill-posed nature of the problem. By applying these methodologies, the study claims that bias is significantly mitigated, resulting in a near-perpendicular component. This outcome has significant implications for observing platforms, with the study suggesting a divergence from current practices for the Yellowknife telescope and considering novel strategies for future instruments.

This research paper explores a real-world scenario in which consumers selfishly aim to minimize their energy bills by scheduling their energy usage in advance. To effectively persuade these consumers to use less energy during peak hours and fairly compensate them, we developed a novel billing scheme that instantiates real-time energy consumption charges. Initially, we define an aggregative game to simulate how these consumers strategically interact with one another, after which we identify the conditions necessary for the game's Nash equilibrium to exist and reach a stable outcome. To address these consumers' collective actions, we propose and demonstrate two promising billing strategies. Firstly, we demonstrate that by imposing a flat monthly fee plus a per-unit energy charge with peak-hour surcharge, consumers can reach equilibrium and, more importantly, reduce overall and individual energy demands during peak hours. Secondly, we find that by appropriately adjusting the ratio between the energy charge and billing fee in instant-time billing, these consumers can reach equilibrium and, more importantly, decrease both aggregate and individual energy consumption during peak hours at the low cost of a small end-time billing variation.

The generalized form of the Einstein theory, the Rastall theory of gravity, incorporates the law of conservation of energy and momentum. We derive a charged black string solution under Rastall theory's framework and subsequently investigate thermal Hawking radiation under this theory. The radiation thermalization is unaffected by Rastall theory's parameters, but the theory modifies the charged black string's mass and its associated Hawking temperature. Consequently, the radiation's energy and spin characteristics exhibit variations due to the altered temperature. Notably, the radiation's energy and spin behaviors distinguish the Rastall theory, where Hawking temperature increases for a non-rotating black string but decreases for a rapidly rotating one.

The results demonstrate that the power-law decay rates found in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem for discrete systems directly correspond to pointwise scaling rates of a spectral measure with a spectral value of one. Moreover, assuming weak convergence, when no spectral gap is present, the convergence rates of the time-average in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem rely on sequences of infinite time as they tend to infinity.

The research on extremely old and metal-poor stars within our Galaxy is instrumental in grasping its chemical evolution and the origin of star formation. These stars are rare, and only five have been detected so far with a metal content below -4.0. Recent data release from Gaia, which covers light from these faint stars, offers a valuable resource. A method has been developed to identify metal-poor stars based on the ratios of blue and red light emitted by these stars, and which require the least amount of luminosity. This approach has been tested using computer simulations and a study of stars with measured properties, resulting in the successful identification of 85% of the most metal-poor stars studied. Moreover, it has been discovered that slightly less metal-rich stars from the same family can also be detected using this method. Next steps involve reviewing the collection of stars identified and conducting follow-up observations to measure the absorption lines of these stars directly, making it feasible to maybe discover additional metal-poor stars which can aid in understanding the chemical evolution of our Galaxy.

This research splits the Earth into a grid of hexagonal cells to collect and analyze worldwide data on daily fire counts from each cell to evaluate seasonal fire severity, defined as accumulated detections per season. The primary aim of this investigation is to assess the accuracy of time series forecasting models using historical active fire data for short and medium-term predictions. This straightforward approach utilizes globally accessible data to facilitate scalable prediction, independent of location or region. The time series forecasting technique utilised offers advantages in adaptability, simplicity, and efficiency by leveraging readily available observations to make predictions. The code is accessible on GitHub for implementation, and results demonstrate substantial accuracy gains over existing methodologies. The time series forecasting technique has also been proven effective on a smaller test dataset in the United States for medium-term predictions up to two years ahead.

We've conducted a thorough examination of eight distinct methods for evaluating the morphological intricacy of languages. These measures have different prerequisites for data annotation, yet our study identifies both similarities and disparities among them. We compare the methods visually and statistically to ascertain how they correlate with typological characteristics. This investigation seeks to determine whether these metrics assess the same underlying aspect of language or, alternatively, measure different facets of morphological complexity. The results from principal component analysis suggest that two of the methods track the same variable, while the others appear to measure distinct aspects of the data.

Researchers at Meneghetti et al recently suggested that strong gravitational lensing, which allows for the discovery of dwarf dwarf galaxies, might be less potent on a small scale than previously thought if dark matter is composed of self-interacting particles. Our investigation assesses the impact of non-baryonic matter self-interactions on the lens equation, reaching the conclusion that such self-interactions do not have a noticeable effect on magnification in cases involving either strong or weak gravitational lensing. This outcome indicates that strong gravitational lensing, which is able to detect faint dwarf galaxies, operates with the same level of potency as weak gravitational lensing, thus expanding our capacity to discover dwarf galaxies across galaxy clusters. This finding might be utilized to determine if dark matter is composed of self-interacting particles by comparing the numbers of detectable sources with and without strong gravitational lensing, within a range of source magnifications, within a specified velocity framework. Our calculations illustrate an implemented example for velocity intervals of $0.01-32, 64 km/s$.

This research focuses on reducing the complexity of parametric partial differential equations (PPDEs) by finding an accurate approximation space for the solutions of the equations. Given incomplete information, we use two primary sources: initial assumptions about the solutions and partial measurements from the equations. Based on these sources, we have developed methods to generate effective approximation subspaces and analyzed their performance. By identifying the optimal performance limit and providing simplified methods to achieve it, we have made strides in addressing the challenges associated with reducing the dimensionality of PPDE solutions while accounting for incomplete information about the equations and their solutions.

This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach ('m-ar-K-FastICA') for feature extraction, combining kernel-based dimensionality reduction with ICA to overcome the limitations of previous methods. Although the kernel trick offers a powerful way to tackle non-linearity, its effectiveness can be undermined by a lack of open-source and reproducible kernel implementations, especially in complex datasets. The proposed m-ar-K-FastICA approach uses a readily available and adaptable Python library that facilitates collaboration with scikit-learn, providing a more reliable solution for feature extraction even in data sets with high entropy levels and no need for data pre-whitening. Several classification experiments using open-access datasets from diverse domains have shown significant performance improvements, showcasing the enhanced capabilities of the proposed approach. Furthermore, a comparison with other widely-used feature extraction methods has validated its superiority in terms of accuracy and reliability.

Identifying trending social media events in real-time across various geographical locations is crucial for processing massive data over spatio-temporal regions. The primary aim is to track events as they unfold and converge at specific locations. For this purpose, an event is defined as a sequence of social media posts linked to a specific location, occurring within a defined time frame, exceeding a specified threshold. The event aggregation approach is enhanced through the application of two geospatial algorithms: Kruskal's and Spanner, employing a balanced map-reduce framework to optimize performance and efficiency. The proposed solution demonstrates effective analysis and resolution of its limitations in processing large-scale social media data. Its robust capabilities allow for accurate trend identification across multiple events, locations, and timeframes. The system's scalability and efficiency have been validated by testing it on social media platforms, such as Twitter and Google+, and various geographical locations like NYC and Paris.

We establish the optimal Lipschitz regularity of very weak solutions for the measure-valued elliptic PDE $-\mathrm{div}(A(x) \nabla u) = Q \; \mathcal{H}^{n-1} \llcorner \Gamma$ within a smooth domain $\Omega$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Here, $\Gamma$ represents a $C^{1, \alpha}$-smooth hypersurface, with $Q$ defined as a $3 \times 3$ symmetric, $L^2(\Gamma)$-integrable tensor, and $A$ constitutes a uniformly elliptic matrix with components in $C^{0} (\overline{\Omega})$.

Advanced permanent magnets made from rare earth and transition metal alloys achieve high magnetization due to high transition metal content. By applying evolutionary search to the yttrium-cobalt-boron system, researchers discovered yttrium cobalt boride compounds with a high cobalt content. This search involved combining experimental and theoretical data sources to create a comprehensive database of the system's composition. From this data, multiple cobalt-rich yttrium cobalt boride compounds were identified, primarily consisting of the YCo$_{16}$B$_{8}$ phase, despite most known compounds having lower cobalt content.

In the field of display advertising, real-time bidding has become the primary approach to buying ad inventory. Each ad impression has a unique price and the goal of an advertiser is to achieve the maximum ROI by bidding the optimal amount. However, the optimal bidding strategy is hindered by the advertiser's daily spending limit and the stochastic nature of ad quality. Existing literature often overlooks these factors, focusing instead on a single expected random variable. This paper proposes a new ROI-based bidding model that takes into account the advertiser's budget and risk sensitivity. Our model can adapt to any pre-defined budget and is sensitive to risk through a regulatory factor. Its bidding amount is directly proportional to ROI and is capped by the budget, limited by a fraction of the ROI multiplied by the spending limit. This ensures the advertiser meets their pre-defined budget and minimizes losses by only spending a fraction of the potential budget. Our model has been thoroughly tested and the results show it outperforms state-of-the-art models under various scenarios.

Nonclassical properties in continuous-variable quantum systems can be measured by quantum steering, which reflects their influence on the target field in quantum teleportation. Recent studies have linked the quantum steering capacity to Wigner negativity, and specifically, the amount of Wigner negativity can serve as a measure of quantum steering. Though this connection was proven for specific measures of Wigner negativity, the relationship remains unverified in multiple definitions of Wigner negativity. We present new proofs for several definitions, in addition to one definition not previously covered by the study, which confirm that different definitions of Wigner negativity yield the same lower bound for quantum steering. We have also demonstrated that one of the unverified definitions of Wigner negativity provides an exponential increase in quantum steering capacity compared to the standard definition.

Accurate secure boundary analysis is crucial for practical quantum key distribution systems, but the current approach overlooks a critical aspect – the randomness consistency of seeds used in privacy amplification. We introduce a novel method to establish a tighter correlation between quantum and classical entropies at the final stage of quantum key distribution by generating many uniform random bits. This technique yields a more precise and manageable analysis, effectively reducing the exclusion of low entropy contributions. As a result, this approach ensures that all remaining quantum entropies after privacy amplification are negligible. We present a practical application of this method in a basic quantum key distribution system, demonstrating its efficacy in enhancing analysis precision.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space.

We'll examine the diffusion process described by the equation $u_t(t, x) =
\tfrac{1}{2}\{x u(t, x)\}_{xx} - \alpha \{x u(t, x)\}_{x}$ with $u(0, x) =
\delta(x - x_0)$ for $t, x, \alpha \ge 0$, initially derived and solved by Feller
for modeling independently reproducing population growth, focusing on related
coalescent processes. We derive the probability distribution for $A_n(s, t)$,
which denotes the number of ancestors at time $s$ in the past of a sample of size
$n$ from the population at time $t$. This leads to two practical applications:
firstly, we obtain expressions for sampling distributions in samples of size
$n$ from a population of independently reproducing organisms at time $t$. In
addition, we relate our results to problems of finding the probability
distribution of the time to the most recent common ancestor (TRCAt) and the last
common ancestor (LCAt) in a sample of size $n$ from a population of time $t$.
These results are represented graphically.

In this work, we explore diagrammatic methods in waveguide QED systems with a particular focus on systems utilizing delayed coherent quantum feedback. By using a specific mathematical approach within the rotating wave approximation, we demonstrate that N-photon scattering matrices in single-qubit systems can be expressed as a combination of (N-1) photon effective Hamiltonian's diagrammatic series. This relationship enables us to compare the scattering matrices of isolated qubits to those of coupled qubits using diagrammatic series expansions. Furthermore, we examine the application of feedback self-consistency conditions to derive exact solutions for complex systems. This involves using a self-consistent diagrammatic method in vacuum, resulting in the exact solution for single-mode single-photon scattering and the approximate solution for two-photon scattering. This method's conditions and achievements are found to be consistent with known exact solutions in both cases. These findings are highly relevant to current waveguide QED experiments that utilize single-emitter systems.
