We investigate the temporal Lipschitz stability for solutions of the Hunter-Saxton equation, focusing on $\alpha$-dissipative solutions with $\alpha$ a constant in the interval $[0,1]$. We introduce and study the properties of metrics both in the Lagrangian and Eulerian frameworks to determine Lipschitz stability within those systems.

Evaluating scoliosis with ultrasound imaging is particularly difficult for individuals without prior experience. A newly developed robotic scanning technique combines deep learning with controlled pressure to accurately follow spinal curvature. This method was tested by 15 healthy subjects to assess its reliability. Both robotic and manual scanning techniques were used simultaneously by each subject, and the consistency between these measurements indicates that the robotic scanning method is a viable option for scoliosis detection, showing a high level of agreement between controlled and manual scans with respect to spinous process displacement. This reliability was also observed in repeated assessments made by five individuals using the robotic scanning method.

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on non-negative integers and is inherently unsupervised. We compare its performance to a median-based ground truth duration model and find that a model trained on median duration values yield comparable results. Moreover, this new approach offers enhanced scalability due to its ability to synthesize at a lower time resolution than the original data, effectively mitigating the data sparse issue. We conduct a listener preference test and observe a substantial 45% increase in preferred utterances from this new model over a baseline that combines a phoneme-based model with median-corrected duration information.

Identifying online hate speech is increasingly critical due to its capacity to inflict emotional and psychological harm on minority groups. A recent study from TU Berlin's research team analyzed the performance of different Natural Language Processing models on subtasks one and two of the 2021 Indo-European language shared task, which focused on detecting hate speech and derogatory content. Our team assessed the effectiveness of models that rely on word and character-based recurrent neural networks and those employing transfer learning via BERT, all of which utilized a shared task dataset. It was discovered that models applying transfer learning outperformed others across both tasks.

Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) neural networks have been shown to surpass their non-MIMO counterparts in visual recognition tasks, such as image classification, due to their ability to learn task-specific correlations between inputs. However, traditional MIMO networks are hindered by their limited capacity for accommodating multiple inputs effectively. This limitation stems from the standard practice of sharing features across inputs using a single shared encoder. In an effort to rectify this issue, a novel method for feature sharing in MIMO networks is introduced, specifically designed to identify and leverage the unique correlations between individual inputs. By implementing this approach, MIMO networks are able to tap into a richer source of information, and as such, it is anticipated that it will enhance the performance of these models in tasks involving visual understanding, and potentially beyond. Experimental results indicate a notable increase in task accuracy for a range of classification and segmentation tasks.

This study undertakes a comprehensive analysis of existing datasets pertinent to the analysis of historical documents through image-based techniques. Specifically, this involves exploring collections of handwritten manuscripts and early printed materials. Acquiring suitable datasets for research on historical documents employing various machine learning methodologies necessitates identifying appropriate datasets. Though numerous document image datasets have been developed over the years, there is a notable absence of a unified literature survey on this subject. To address this gap, this research aims to catalog a broad range of datasets tailored to the investigation of historical documents. Moreover, this work initiates an in-depth examination of the applicability of pre-trained deep learning architectures to the analysis of historical documents.

Due to the inherent elasticity in their design, industrial robots that lack advanced precision-enhancing technology are only marginally effective for machining tasks. Besides issues related to structure, temperature, and support bearings, one major factor behind elasticity is the backlash in the transmission systems. This study proposes a method for improving trajectory precision using supplementary sensors in robotic joints. Our framework relies on the rather straightforward concept of a divided circle, which is then combined with a novel flatness-based control approach to address the backlash impact. To demonstrate the efficacy and practicality of this method, numerical simulations and real-world experiments on a Scorlet-3D robot were conducted, yielding promising results that show the practical applicability of this approach in contemporary robotic systems.

The study of how chronic diseases evolve throughout an individual's lifetime is crucial in understanding disease management and prevention.  This "life course health trajectory" concept cannot be adequately analyzed using the traditional single-record approach of most medical studies.  Instead, a new method, Multiple State Analysis, accurately captures the changes in disease status over time, allowing researchers to model the effects of risk factors on multiple, simultaneous outcomes.  This research validates the use of this approach in a new, realistic simulation study and then examines the impact of modifiable risk factors on long-term health in individuals who have had a heart attack.  Using data from over 1,500 patients at the University of California, San Francisco, researchers created models to understand how factors such as high blood pressure, smoking, and dietary habits influence subsequent heart attacks, strokes, and rehospitalizations.  In total, over 7,000 future events were included in this analysis, demonstrating the efficiency of this approach for understanding complex patterns of disease.

One widely accepted method for evaluating the electronic energy of large complexes involving thousands of atoms is the density functional theory with a plane-wave and a finite-element approach as its subset. In this context, thorough research has been conducted on efficient methods for evaluating the electronic energy, particularly with the Poincaré-Altoufie summation formula, but the accuracy of these methods has not been thoroughly examined. Our study focuses on evaluating the accuracy of this formula, especially when applied to complex structures, by incorporating multi-center quadrature schemes. We present and discuss two schemes: the first using a single quadrature formula for all functions, and the second with separate quadrature formulas for kinetic and potential energy components. Our results show that the second method has the highest precision. We further investigate the effectiveness of pre-computed tablues and the impact of the quadrature scheme on the error using statistical methods, and conclude that the precision of the Poincaré-Altoufie method is sufficient for many applications, and combining it with pre-computed tablues and an optimized quadrature scheme provides highly accurate results, even for complex structures.

In a graph, a subset of vertices forms a resolving set if, for any two vertices, a single set vertex is positioned at different distances from the two vertices. The problem of finding a resolving set of size at most k, called the Metric Dimension problem, has been a subject of research since the 1970s. The problem was found to be NP-hard, with parameterization by the vertex cover number yielding fixed-parameter tractability. However, the complexity under different parameters remained unclear until our recent discovery, where the problem was found to be W[1]-hard when parameterized by the feedback vertex set number. Additionally, we found that parameterization by the vertex cover number results in the problem not admitting a polynomial kernel unless a significant assumption holds. While the problem remains open under the vertex cover number, we found fixed-parameter tractability when parameterizing the problem by distance to cluster or co-cluster.

Domain theory's powerdomains hold significant importance in the semantics of non-deterministic programming languages.  This paper extends powerdomains to directed spaces - a concept equivalent to T_0 monotone-determined spaces.  Powerdomain-like spaces of directed spaces were created through the use of an upper powerdomain and a generalized version of powerdomains known as least fixed points of monotone operators over directed spaces.  It was proven that these spaces often have distinct structures and that various directed space powerdomain constructions are represented as the fixed points of certain monotone operators.  Notably, it was discovered that upper powerdomains are used in T_0 monotone-determined spaces while formal Gurulab powerdomains are a special case of the least fixed points of monotone operators in directed spaces.  This work also provides the basis for further investigations into abstract powerdomains of directed spaces.

Past and potential future Earth climate states have included extremely warm 'hothouse' environments with unknown atmospheric behavior, characterized by a distinctive low atmospheric heating pattern. In contrast to typical cooling effects, 'hothouse' climates are distinguished by a blocked window region for water vapor, which has led to theories of resulting temperature inversions and altered cloud formations. Prior studies using atmospheric radiation models suggested 'hothouse' climates would experience increased precipitation, but a reliable observation network has yet to be established, and the predicted increases were calculated using radiative models. These were shown to be flawed in a previous study and this research extends it by exploring precipitation patterns in 'hothouse' climates. It reveals a more complex climate dynamics, featuring heavy downpours and cold surface-water interactions that have implications for future flooding risks.

We've established an inverse Penrose transform for self-dual Yang-Mills theory and its spin-off variants in a flat space environment. The spin-off variant's twistor action fits within the broader BF framework. When we deviated from the standard self-dual sector of this variant, we stumbled upon a novel action describing a higher-spin theory. This theory stems from a self-contained sector of a twistor action and features Yang-Mills fields with complex spin properties. A comprehensive analysis, encompassing the free theory, classical field equations, and linearized action recovery, confirms our initial findings. Our work introduces a BF-based framework for twistor construction in higher-spin theory, offering fresh insights into these theories and their underlying action labels.

The application of deep neural networks in medical image analysis has shown significant potential due to their advanced capabilities in complex tasks, yet their reliance on a vast dataset marked by inconsistent quality has resulted in inconsistent performance across various medical disciplines. To effectively extract insights from a noisy medical dataset, we introduce a novel labeling mechanism built on a Bayesian statistics framework, which effectively rectifies label noise by assessing the balance between a model's learning accuracy and classification precision. Our method entails an updated objective function that differentiates between correct and incorrect class labels, leveraging the principles of the Dirichlet posterior distribution and the Bayesian high-dimensional Bayes estimator. We rigorously analyze the theoretical learning outcomes of our mechanism and validate its effectiveness through experiments involving standard medical datasets for various deep learning tasks.

Consider a unit cube, $Q_n$, in $n$-dimensional space and a function space, $C(Q_n)$, consisting of continuous functions from $Q_n$ to $\mathbb{R}$. Define the norm of the interpolation projector $P_i$ mapping $C(Q_n)$ to $C(Q_n)$ with respect to a given point set $I$ as $\|P_i\| = \sup \{\|P_i(f)\|_{C(Q_n}} \over \||f\|_{C(Q_n}} \over}$ for any function $f$ in $C(Q_n}$. Here, the induced norm is defined as $\|f\|_{C(Q_n}}$ = $\sup\{\|f(x)\|_{\mathbb{R}}: x \in Q_n}$. We estimate the least upper bound of the norm $\|P_i\|$ for a given cardinality $|I| = N$ and find the order of the error in this estimate.

A correlated random walk (CRW) developing on a connected finite graph G counts the number of a walker's steps n, where l(n) denotes these steps and W(n) represents the walker's position at step n, considered a stochastic matrix. This matrix's eigenvalues were found to be real and its characteristic polynomial was determined when the graph is undirected and symmetric by D.A. Ganesan. However, in directed graphs or those not following a rejection-free policy, the stochastic matrix is distinct and so are its eigenvalues and the characteristic polynomial, particularly when the graph is non-homogeneous or non-regular. This paper's objective is to investigate these eigenvalues and the characteristic polynomial in such cases by introducing a concept called 'adjusted multiplicative factors for eigenvalues associated with arbitrary directed graphs or those not following a rejection-free policy, described as Z(G,W).

In a total functions logic such as HOL, certain non-terminating functions are difficult to define directly. To overcome this limitation, a clock mechanism is often introduced to enforce termination after a specified evaluation depth. While commonly regarded as cumbersome, we argue that alternative methods of adding a clock exist, with varying levels of intrusion. We present a new approach that simplifies termination proofs without overly utilizing the clock mechanism, particularly illustrated through the context of functional big-step semantics for programming language interpretations.

The accuracy of models predicting the spatial arrangement of instantaneously occurring wall-bound flow is heavily reliant on the geometric characteristics of the representative structures they employ. This study aims to establish a new approach for identifying the 3-D geometric characteristics of significant, swirling motions within wall-bound, turbulent flows, along with their size and location. This approach can be used in conjunction with existing models that describe these coherent structures to improve our understanding of these complex flows. Furthermore, the combination of data-driven methods and structure-based models offers a potential solution for increasing the predictive accuracy of existing models.

This study demonstrates the presence of self-dual (topological) solitons within a modified baby Skyrme model that incorporates Born-Infeld term governed gauge field behavior. The effective implementation of the Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield framework yields an energy lower bound, with corresponding self-dual equations whose solutions manifest as the limiting solitons that achieve this bound. The lower bound on energy, known as the Bogomol'nyi bound, may be denoted as E_B, with the actual energy E exceeding or equal to this bound (E >= E_B). The research reveals that for specific parameters, these self-dual solitons result in a configuration where the energy assumes its minimal value (E = E_B), displaying stability and exhibiting topological properties. The solutions to the self-dual equations also illustrate the domain wall, gauge field, and Hopf map properties associated with this model.

For a square lattice with a magnetic field whose flux is a irrational number divided, Weyl semimetals are found to exhibit semimetallic behavior regardless of the direction of the spin. However, when this magnetic field's flux is irrational, an extensive analysis reveals that each spin orientation hosts an infinite number of semimetals, and the total number of semimetals for both spin orientations is given by the formula $N_{\mathrm{semi-metal}}=2\sum_{k\geq1}\left(\zeta(2k)+(-1)^{2k}\zeta(2k-1)\right)2^{-\lceil2k/3\rceil}$. These semimetals were found to exhibit nontrivial scaling behavior in the absence of a charge gap, and the results show that time-reversal-broken Weyl semimetals can be found even in strong magnetic fields for any irrational magnetic flux. Additionally, numerical calculations confirm the existence of these semimetals, and the findings show that they form quasi-periodic chains in the bulk at sufficiently large magnetic field strength. These chains are found to extend along a diagonal in a quasi-one-dimensional arrangement.

This research paper introduces an advanced optical nanoantenna design, consisting of a hybrid silicon nanoring coupled with a localised assembly of quantum dots, which together constitute an efficient source of photons. The study demonstrates how this arrangement can achieve increased radiance and enhanced photonic emission rates due to its ability to efficiently couple light and unidirectional photon release. The designed nanoantenna exhibits optimal performance when illuminated by light of a specific polarisation, thereby enhancing its capabilities as a bright and unidirectional photon source. The research has implications for future improvements in optical quantum entanglement experiments and measurements, particularly those requiring low phonon loss levels.

Mechanical screening, a widely observed phenomenon in various materials and systems, is well understood when considering standard screening theories. However, in certain contexts involving discrete particles or fractures, these theories fail, leading researchers to propose anomalous screening theories that address specific challenges. Yet, these proposed theories have not been extensively validated across different scenarios. To shed light on this, a study investigated mechanical screening under various conditions using both experimental and computational methods in a specific context. The research involved manipulating a granular column under different weights above a detector and monitoring the screen's propagation. Screening times were compared with and without introducing an additional mass on the screen. The results indicated that standard screening theories accurately describe the behavior under examined conditions and showed that proposed anomalous theories do not apply in this specific scenario. However, the study found that mechanical friction plays a crucial role in determining the screening process. The researchers developed a numerical model based on particle interactions and analyzed hysteresis in granular systems, which aligns with experimental findings. Furthermore, introducing a slight tilt to the screen led to increased mechanical complexity, causing additional friction to dominate the behavior. The researchers suggested that effective screening algorithms should consider discrete particle systems and their local friction properties rather than relying on simplified models.

Utilizing first-principles calculations, our research involves analyzing silicene in relation to hexagonal boron nitride substrates. Hexagonal boron nitride, being a semiconductor, has weaker interactions with silicene in comparison to metallic substrates. As a result, silicene's band gap can potentially be expanded up to 50 meV. Additionally, the impact of manganese decoration on the system is explored by calculating the onsite Hubbard interaction parameter, which significantly differs between decoration at the top and hollow sites. Furthermore, the system's induced magnetism is thoroughly examined.

The Sgr A East supernova remnant, located near the center of the Milky Way, poses a mystery with age estimates ranging from extremely young, around 1-2 thousand years, to a significantly older, 10 thousand year estimate. Our objective is to create a straightforward simulation of a supernova event replicating the observed exterior dimensions and aspects of the Sgr A East remnant. Achieving this would provide insight to answer the question: What kind of supernova occurred in the vicinity of the Galactic center? A comprehensive examination is performed, considering diverse physical conditions such as the supernova's location, the density of surrounding material, and the distribution of magnetic fields. Remnant shapes and scales are evaluated in three dimensions, taking into account external factors such as the Galactic wind's effect on the supernova, using 1D, 2D, and 3D models. These analyses account for factors like the movement of the galaxy and the interplay of surrounding gas within the galactic center. Our results suggest that a Type II supernova, landing on the iron-rich SiC-rich zone but missing the carbon-rich zone within the red giant branch of the star, best explains Sgr A East's observed characteristics. However, an older age of around 10 thousand years is more consistent with a larger initial supernova size. It's estimated that in the vicinity of the galactic center, the initial explosion pressure is around 5-10 billion Pascals. Additionally, the mystery

The study examines various oversampling methods to classify multi-class topics, particularly focusing on the performance of SMOTE, a popular method for generating new samples based on minority class instances, and its two variants along with random oversampling in text classification tasks. The research assesses the efficiency of SMOTE, its Borderline and ADASYN modifications, and random oversampling in conjunction with machine learning algorithms such as k-nearest neighbor, support vector machine, and different types of neural networks, on datasets formed by combining multiple topics. The results reveal that oversampling enhances the accuracy of KNN, SVM, and neural networks, with the former methods demonstrating superior performance compared to random oversampling. Furthermore, the research finds that Borderline oversampling exhibits better outcomes compared to both SMOTE and ADASYN, indicating the potential of using a more stringent method to improve classification tasks.

This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct dataset of over 750,000 articles from over 300 outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID at a higher rate when cases were rising in their surrounding counties. However, our analysis reveals that news outlets in counties hit hard by the pandemic were slower to report on COVID deaths. We also found that local news outlets in counties with higher COVID mortality rates during the 2020 election targeted political content aimed at certain voter groups. Furthermore, our research indicates that COVID coverage by local news is more closely linked to news audience size than to county population size. Ultimately, our findings shed light on how local news outlets responded to COVID, revealing the complex interplay between COVID coverage, community COVID severity, and news audience characteristics.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless when accurately integrated, maintaining machine-precise levels of total mass, energy, and linear/angular momentum conservation. Notably, this property holds significant value in computational astrophysics for processes such as binary interactions and compact objects' evolution. Although the inclusion of gravity in such applications leads to excessive computation in pairwise interactions, a Fast Multipole Method variant addresses this by substituting interactions between distant particle clusters, which however introduces inaccuracies in angular momentum conservation. Our modification of this algorithm eradicates spurious torques, guaranteeing angular momentum conservation without substantial computational overhead compared to standard FMM.

Numerical studies have been conducted on the $Q^2$ dependence of cross-sectional ratios in electron proton collisions, drawing on JLab polarization experiments measuring the ratio of Sachs form factors in such interactions. Specifically, the $10 ^2 $ to $10 ^4 $ MeV $^2$ Q $^2$ range was examined, focusing on the JPsi polynomial model's predictions. This led to a discovery that cross-sectional ratios do not consistently indicate the ratio of proton electromagnetic form factors. Calculations also showed a significant, approximately 20% $ longitudinal to transverse $ cross-sectional ratio in electron proton collisions, even at high $ Q^2$, as opposed to 2:1, indicating partial transfer of initial proton polarization to the final proton. This outcome may explain the excessive polarization observed in $ ^6He + p \to e ^- + e ^+ + p $ interactions.

We develop a non-conservative method for augmenting observation space to enhance robustness against perturbations and improve transfer learning between related tasks. This approach involves identifying a task-specific 'expert' model that maximizes expected return within a given state; it then seeks to find the most effective transformation to apply to the current observation, making it similar to a new state where the expert model maximizes return. This goal is achieved through an iterative process using a mixture of two distributions: the current observation and the optimized state image. This procedure expands the search space, enabling the method to achieve return levels up to 69% of the baseline in a challenging multi-task experiment where transfer is difficult. This comparative figure rises to 98% when the tasks are more closely related. Notably, the efficiency of our method scales sub-quadratically with the number of training samples. Moreover, the method demonstrates robustness against perturbations, utilizing an arbitrarily chosen characteristic for augmentation. Finally, the method exhibits properties analogous to contrastive learning in the context of supervised learning from expert models.

A comprehensive study of the creation of two Higgs bosons ($hh$) paired with a vector boson ($V$) has been investigated, using a vast dataset collected by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider between 2015 and 2018 in a proton-proton collision energy of 13 TeV, equivalent to 139 inverse femtobarns of data. The diverse combinations of $V$ (which can be a Z or a W boson) and the two Higgs boson states with non-zero mass have been examined. The presence of the $ZZ*$ or $ZZ$ processes generating comparable signatures is accounted for in the analysis. By thoroughly examining signals from the $Z~h~h$, $Z~ZZ$, $W~hh$, and $Z~ZZ$ processes, using a Bayesian estimation with 136 inverse femtobarns of data, no significant anomalies were detected that cannot be explained by the standard model. This led to setting new, strict bounds on the coupling of the Higgs boson to other bosons. Furthermore, the study provides a comparison of expected versus observed errors in the coupling of the Higgs boson to other bosons in the $\sin^2 \theta_W$ parameter at 95% confidence level, with slight variations depending on the specific process under examination.

Atomic magnetometers based on optical or radio-frequency detection have become the most advanced devices for measuring magnetic fields. Yet, no version has been created that can maintain precise field measurements over an extensive area - over one meter wide, for example. The key limitation has been the lower light intensity and decreased number of detectable atoms in such systems. Consequently, developers have to find a way to enhance light coupling, specifically "coherently" to facilitate the production of stable magnetic fields, while also combating potential noise factors along the way. The data shown here presents a fully digital method for creating a system that can synchronize the light used for such magnetometers and for accurately transferring instructions to modulate them digitally. The digital method works by coherently combining the light emitted by thousands of cesium atoms using either a fiber or a thin glass tube and then manipulating this light to produce a maser signal at a specific frequency. The signal can then be used to produce extremely precise magnetic fields over a very large area - over one meter wide, for example. The digital method also allows for the use of more advanced digital processing techniques to create and modify such magnetic fields, specifically for the production of square or triangular fields along the way. The ability to produce such digital magnetic fields along such large areas also allows for the demonstration of the coherence of the system along such large areas. The digital method can also be applied to more advanced digital processing techniques, specifically for the production of magnetic fields along specific shapes, such as squares or

For K3 surfaces with an automorphism having a Siegel disk, the associated Picard number falls between $0$ and $18$ and must be an even integer. Conversely, applying the technique of hypergeometric groups, K3 surface automorphisms possessing Siegel disks can be constructed to demonstrate all conceivable Picard numbers through the identification and computation of relevant algebraic numbers derived from Lefschetz-type formulas and their corresponding residues.

A supergravity unified framework neutralino is proposed as a plausible candidate for dark matter, where a long-lived neutralino decays into the hidden sector's lightest supersymmetric particle, exceeding the age of the universe. We introduce an extension to the MSSM/SUGRA model with a $U(1)_{X_1} \times U(1)_{X_2}$ hidden sector gauge sector, where the hidden sector neutralino is lighter than its visible counterpart, leading to a loop-suppressed radiative decay process. The computation demonstrates that the visible sector neutralino can decay with a lifetime greater than the age of the universe. The detectability of this scenario lies in the indirect observation of a long-lived neutralino, manifested as nuclear recoils or gamma-ray emissions from decays within or outside the galaxy's core, such as in the Crab nebula or galactic gas and inverse Compton scattering.

The main contributions of this study include developing an Efficient Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme for finding the minimum surface topography (genus and Euler characteristics) for dense graphs. In particular, for graphs with n vertices and density d (or more specifically, the number of edges), we can calculate a surface topography that has at most O(n^2 log n) faces and bounded curvature, and can be embedded in a 3D sphere of similar volume, all within polynomial time with respect to n, regardless of d's value. This solution builds upon our previous algorithm that identified a faceable surface for any dense graph in near-linear time. Additionally, we can calculate a surface topography with the minimum possible Euler characteristics in polynomial time as well. This result addresses an open problem first highlighted by Chazal et al. in 2009.

A stochastic Newton algorithm for distributed convex optimization tasks is proposed, which utilizes individual machine capabilities to calculate gradient and Hessian-vector products for the same objective through parallel processing. Convergence analysis and performance preservation are achieved by a consensus algorithm that enables synchronized convergence of each machine's estimates towards the collective solution. We demonstrate that under certain conditions, the algorithm's convergence rate remains identical to its centralized counterpart, supporting the notion of 'distributed efficiency without sacrifice.' Empirical evaluations using a synthetic dataset demonstrate the algorithm's efficacy in real-world applications.

Our approach to training a neural network to identify hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali is outlined in this work. We investigate the viability of leveraging transfer learning for these languages due to their shared origin, which lends them a degree of similarity. Our experiment's implementation on low-powered hardware yields results that hold up against those of more costly models, a noteworthy finding. Additionally, given the limited training data and our unfamiliarity with these languages, our study represents an attempt to decipher languages often shrouded in mystery.

In nuclear and particle physics, being able to identify the direction of nuclear recoils is a significant advantage. This capability, achievable at low energies, could help verify that a dark matter signal comes from dark matter, differentiate between various neutrino sources, or identify neutron beta decay. With sufficient readout detail, such as 0.1 mm resolution over a 1 cm drift length, this becomes possible even with common TPC gases, thanks to the high spatial resolution offered by Gas Time Projection Chambers. Determining the direction of recoiling nuclei is feasible due to the minor variation in ion drift velocity caused by kinetic energy. Four potential indicators of this variation are examined: dE/dx, Time, Drift, and Physics Signal Slop Analysis. Our study involves simulating experiments with electron recoils from beta decays and nuclear recoils from nuclear reactions with different kinematics using GEANT4. The results suggest that directional analysis could be an effective way to separate these two types of recoils even when they share the same initial energy, according to various metrics.

A comprehensive analysis of commercial driving behavior requires considering various personal characteristics and environmental influences like weather and road conditions. Current driver-assessment systems primarily rely on behavior records, neglecting essential contextual factors. To create a more comprehensive evaluation system that accounts for all relevant information, we propose an innovative method. This approach involves using machine learning to gather data from diverse sources and then incorporating expert input to ensure fairness in the assessment process. By merging human knowledge and machine learning, our system can provide a more accurate and unbiased assessment of commercial drivers, ultimately leading to enhanced safety on the roads.

This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,864,405 text instances.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic approach to reading full text and a focused task of identifying individual words.
The analysis of baseline models and those submitted by competitors revealed a significant disparity between the two in terms of accuracy.
Future research initiatives will focus on addressing market-oriented issues to establish more practical OCR solutions.

Random fields in mathematical models depict how interconnected random variables behave over time, influencing a variety of disciplines from statistical physics to system biology. Since their introduction by Erdoes 1925, [2] in a non-rigorous framework, the concept of random field connectivity has gained traction with Steiglitz 1960, [3] presenting a rigorous proof for a specific case. This paper delves into the geometry of Gaussian fields, examining the concept of shortest paths (geodesics) within the associated manifolds. We establish the conditions under which these geodesics exist and provide an exhaustive analysis. Our research also verifies the validity of certain earlier predictions.
In our research, we conduct experiments on Rayleigh-Taylor Instability by introducing a controlled disturbance through magnetic levitation technology.

For a cuspidal Hecke eigenform $F$ of weight $k$ associated with the group $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$, we can derive a finitude theorem for the denominators of the values $L(F, \sigma)(j)$ where $j$ ranges from $1$ to $k+1$, and $\sigma$ is a Dirichlet character. This finding extends previous work by Iwaniec and Sarnak on the finitude of certain Galois module determinants, and also aligns with recent conclusions drawn by Rouvier for weights less than $1$, and by Hartung for even weights greater than $1$.

In a tight binding model using the non-equilibrium Green's functions formalism, researchers explored how spin-dependent transport behaves in armchair graphene nanoribbons with ferromagnetic gate control. The investigation delved into conductance and spin polarization oscillations caused by varying barrier heights, which can be regulated with gate voltages, in addition to analyzing the effects of external gate control on these parameters. The results showed that with proper choice of band gap and effective barrier heights, spin polarization can be controlled and manipulated.

This paper presents proofs of Korovkin theorem analogues in the realm of weakly nonlinear, monotone operators applied to multi-variable Banach lattices of functions. Our study encompasses the almost everywhere convergence, convergence in measure, and $L^{p}$-norm convergence. The discussion is supplemented by several examples that demonstrate the theoretical findings.

A graph on n vertices is called pancyclic if it contains a cycle of every possible length from 3 to n. In 1972, Erdos demonstrated that a graph on n vertices with n larger than 4k has a cycle of length k or close to it. This result was improved by Gerold Moese who proved that such a graph must contain two cycles of consecutive lengths. In the following years, certain conditions were applied to the problem and it was established that a graph with n vertices and its independence number y equals k if it contains a cycle of length k or close to it. In 2012, Yuster proved that a graph with n vertices and its independence number y equals k if it contains a cycle of length k or close to it with at most y-1 vertices. In the given research, it is shown that a graph with n vertices and its independence number y equals k if it contains a Hamiltonian cycle or a pancyclic series of cycles.

The trajectory of light particles created in gold-gold, ruthenium-ruthenium, and zirconium-zirconium collisions at a specific energy level of 200 GeV has been studied in this research. This study utilized the CLVisc model to examine the development of uneven energy density, pressure variations, and radial movement along a specific axis, finding significant relationships among these elements. By comparing data on specific particles to laboratory collisions, researchers discovered that an initial medium imbalance is a primary driver of light particles' trajectory. The uneven initial medium creates opposite forces depending on impact point and collision direction, causing a negative or positive trajectory in certain cases. The direction of light particles emitted at different angles also indicates varying levels of medium imbalance and particle energy, with a negative or positive trajectory in certain cases showing significant relationships with these factors. This research found a correlation between the direction of light particles and their energy, with a negative or positive trajectory in certain cases showing strong connections to specific particles. Finally, comparing data on different collisions showed that isobar collisions at similar centralities have slightly lower medium imbalance than gold-gold collisions, while lower densities result in less significant negative or positive trajectory in certain cases.

The adaptive spectral Koopman method was designed to solve complex autonomous dynamical systems that serve as the groundwork for numerous applications across diverse scientific and engineering fields. Despite its high accuracy, ASK has a computational disadvantage in dealing with multi-dimensional systems compared to traditional integration methods like Runge-Kutta. To address this limitation, we have developed a new approach that combines the ASK method with sparse grid techniques to speed up computation for high-dimensional systems. This new method, known as SASK, uses the Smolyak structure to efficiently construct collocation points and associated polynomials that help approximate Koopman operator eigenfunctions. By optimizing the collocation point selection, SASK achieves a significant reduction in computational cost without compromising the overall error. With the optimization, the method requires only $\mathcal{O}(N^{-1/\alpha})$ grid points to achieve the same error as sparse grid methods for linear problems, resulting in a significant reduction of computational cost by a factor of $\alpha$ for nonlinear problems. To test the method's efficiency, SASK is applied to solve multiple complex systems successfully.

In this paper, the continuous exterior complex scaling method is applied to explain how small non-polar molecules, like helium and carbon monoxide, transition from their non-resonant ground states to long-lived excited states when exposed to a strong DC electric field. The method takes advantage of a numerical technique called the exterior complex scaling method. The excitation paths, called valleys, are calculated using a simple single-channel approach and further validated using a more comprehensive multi-channel approach. The results suggest the existence of deeper valleys that cannot be explained by a simple single-channel model and feature a non-monotonic energy behavior characteristic of a Morse potential. This implies that an atom or molecule in a strong DC electric field can temporarily rest in a metastable state. The estimates for the limits of existence and endpoints of valleys based on an approximate model are surprisingly accurate, considering they are calculated using a simple single-channel approach. The findings also shed light on the practical limitations of a proposed quantum control method, where an atom or molecule in a ground state is pumped into a excited state through a laser pulse. The results suggest that in a certain regime of intensity, the probability of successfully pumping the atom or molecule is very small if it has been pre-conditioned with a strong DC electric field due to the presence of a competing valley that cannot be eliminated by the laser pulse.

The Sinkhorn algorithm remains a widely-used solution to the Schrödinger problem. While it's well-documented that this algorithm converges when a solution exists, a linear convergence rate is achieved only if both the solution and the reference coupling have the same support. Considering the possibility that no solution exists with a particular support, we investigate the algorithm's behavior in this scenario. A theoretical analysis shows that even without a solution, the algorithm can divert towards a linear convergence path if an appropriate initial reference coupling is chosen, specifically one with a smaller support size. Experimentation supports these findings, demonstrating the algorithm can identify multiple solutions of different sizes within the same marginal laws.

The ATLAS experiment at the LHC recorded data of 257 pb-1 in proton-proton collisions at a 5.02 TeV centre-of-mass energy in 2017, which is utilized to determine the t¯t cross-section. The measurement involves both dilepton and single-lepton t¯t final states and yields a combined result. The calculated t¯t cross-section has a total uncertainty of 3.9% and amounts to 67.5 pb, which corresponds to 0.9 pb (statistical) ± 2.3 pb (syst. ± 1.1 (lumi.) pb). This outcome is consistent with theoretical quantum chromodynamic predictions and offers constraints on the proton's parton distribution functions at small x and high scales.

It's logical to assume that the characteristics of a surrounding system or environment would influence the behavior of its core element. Researchers have recently investigated the impact of this influence in the case of a one-dimensional quantum particle coupled to multiple non-interacting fermions in a central potential, and found that the dynamics of the surrounding system are consistent and predictable. The particle's ability to localize is dependent on the characteristics of the surrounding system, and not the other way around. Furthermore, the prediction shows that, under certain conditions, the localization behavior of the surrounding system can be identical to that of the core particle, and it can switch states quickly from localized to delocalized and back. The phenomenon of 'core-loss' occurs when the particle efficiently transfers its energy to the surrounding system, spreading it over a large number of states. Researchers have thoroughly studied this core-loss phenomenon, and have found that it is marked by the suppression of localization and core energy. The suppression is predictable and applies to all core energies, and it can be identified by decreases in certain time-dependent currents.

The conditions on $A$, $B$, $p$, $b$, and $c$ are specified that guarantee 
${u}_{p,b,c}(z)$ meets the requirement ${u}_{p,b,c}(z) \prec (1+Az)/(1+Bz)$. This yields conditions 
for $(-4\kappa/c)({u}_{p,b,c}(z)-1)$, $c \neq 0$, to be close-to-convex and for ${u}_{p,b,c}(z)$ 
to be Janowski convex as well as $z{u}_{p,b,c}(z)$ to be Janowski starlike in the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting a study on the impact of these changes on the diversity of encounters in cities. Analyzing aggregated mobility data from mobile devices in nine cities worldwide, the research found that pandemic measures significantly decreased urban diversity of encounters across all cities, despite varying response policies. Furthermore, this study provides initial evidence of a correlation between diminished diversity of encounters and decreased income diversity in urban areas, indicating that urban diversity is threatened not only by pandemic measures but also by individual behavioral changes.

This research project focuses on the advancement of a nonlinear field-split
preconditioner comprising two stages to expedite convergence of complex two-phase
fluid dynamics and transport within diverse porous media. A proposed algorithm,
Field-Split Multiplicative Schwarz Newton, operates in a sequential two-step process:
initially, an approximate pressure field is generated through Newton's iterations
to address streamline potentials and source-term balancing; secondly, the updated
pressure field is then determined via a Schwarz formulation deeply rooted in
streamline interpolation, which integrates balancing of the streamlines via a
massively relaxed Schwarz method. A thorough comparison between this algorithm and
other nonlinear field-split preconditioners such as FS-MSSM is conducted, with
empirical outcomes derived from solving synthetic and real-world two-phase flow
problems at the core-rock interface and the Ordovician-Hordalian Formations.

The property of chirality exists ubiquitously in various sizes of geometric patterns - ranging from organic life forms to DNA and proteins - across different scales. Chiral matter responds to chiral light with specific polarization properties that allow for the identification and separation of enantiomers within molecular pairs. Developing an optical cavity capable of efficiently interacting with one chiral form of a molecule while rejecting its opposite form is a highly sought-after application in various fields. We successfully designed and created a chiral optical cavity that only supports modes with specific polarization properties, ignoring the opposing modes. Resonant interaction between this cavity and chiral molecules leads to a complete separation of enantiomers into distinct groups. Our proposed approach uses an array of chiral microcylinders arranged in a two-dimensional structure, where all cylinders within a group have the same orientation. We analyzed and validated the chiral properties of individual and groups of cylinders through experimental measurements and found that even at small scales, geometric symmetry gives way to chirality. Our study demonstrates that chiral optical cavities with this specific configuration resonate exclusively with the chiral form of molecules, leaving their opposite forms unaffected. These findings provide valuable insights for developing efficient methods to produce, separate, and identify chiral molecules using optical cavities with this unique property.

This paper examines the connection between Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity on anti de-Sitter spaces and a semi-classical limit of two-dimensional string theory, with c less than 1. We observe that the world-sheet theory of this string theory, comprising a space-like Liouville CFT and a time-like non-rational CFT, exhibits actions and partition functions matching those of the JT gravity model. This match, significantly influenced by boundary terms, extends to annulus amplitudes. We also derive the mapping between the Liouville field and the bulk scalar of the JT gravity model. Furthermore, the paper shows that the boundary Schwarzian theory corresponding to the JT gravity model mirrors a double-scaled matrix integral of the two-dimensional non-rational string theory. This work may facilitate further research into Liouville CFT and non-rational CFT.

A spacetime distortion, or warp bubble, generated by the Alcubierre metric can enable massive objects to achieve global speeds faster than light. This research extends our previous solutions by applying the Einstein equations to the warp drive metric, incorporating both a perfect fluid source and a perfect fluid source with a cosmological constant, resulting in either static or dynamically evolving configurations. These new solutions offer a foundation for understanding how the warp drive spacetime arises from more fundamental matter distributions, enabling a link to be established between the warp drive and other gravitational phenomena.

As urban centers expand, ensuring efficient and effective urban planning and management becomes increasingly crucial to maintain living standards, especially in developing cities, where excessive rainfall poses a threat to lives and property. To mitigate the impact of excessive rainfall and improve urban living conditions, accurate and timely data management and processing are essential components of urban planning and management. To address this need, the GUIDES project focuses on designing, developing, and implementing data engineering solutions to handle rainfall and flood forecasting-related data in an intelligent and real-time manner. By integrating IoT, data analytics, and smart decision support systems, GUIDES aims to enhance rainfall and flood forecasting, ultimately creating a safer urban environment for citizens.

To analyze the center-of-mass motion of hundreds of $^9$Be$^+$ ions, arranged in a two-dimensional Wigner crystal, we utilized the interaction between optical dipoles and the ions' spin, enabling the characterization of their transverse movement. This was done by comparing the experimentally measured effects on spin dephasing with theoretical predictions, resulting in accurate estimations of temperature levels consistent with previously documented standards, including both laser cooling constraints and earlier research methods. Additionally, our approach enabled the differentiation between the ions' initial motion states as either thermal or coherent, providing crucial knowledge for understanding the system. This analysis technique was also adaptable to monitor the incremental increase in mode temperatures over time, thus evaluating the effectiveness of established trapping methods.

TERS is an essential technique for analyzing surfaces with subnanometer resolution. Yet, accurately simulating specific TERS signals is computationally difficult. Our innovative method combines the primary factors driving the effectiveness of TERS, the electromagnetic and chemical interactions, into a single quantum simulation. The electromagnetic influence describes the sample's interaction with highly localized, inhomogeneous electric fields produced by the plasmonic tip, a focal point of many mechanistic studies. Conversely, the chemical interaction accounts for the distinct responses between the apex tip and sample under extremely close-range, highly position-sensitive chemical interactions. Our study focuses on a SnPc sample molecule paired with a single silver atom, modeling the chemical interaction using a time-dependent density functional theory description. By incorporating the electromagnetic influence using a series of point charges simulating the plasmonic Ag nanoparticle, we examine the Raman response across the entire 3D grid, demonstrating the achievable enhancement and resolution under both non-resonant and resonant illumination. Our simulation, encompassing both effects, solidifies the notion that TERS is capable of identifying subtle molecular features.

We used the 64-m Sardinia Radio Telescope to study the emission of nearby spiral galaxies in the K band. Our goal was to detect the Anomalous Microwave Emission (AME) produced by spinning dust grains in the galaxies NGC 3627, NGC 4254, NGC 4736, and NGC 5055, with particular attention to how their emission relates to M 31. Through radio-continuum data and global photometry at 18.6 and 24.6 GHz, we sought to find excess emission due to AME beyond the expected thermal and synchrotron components. Instead of a detection, our research yielded only a upper limit of $S_{\nu}=(2.8\pm2.)\times10^{-2}~\textrm{Jy}~\textrm{sr}^{-1}$ at 18.6 GHz for M 31. Considering the similar radio-continuum properties of our sample galaxies and their expected AME profiles as far-IR-radio correlations, our non-detection suggests that AME might not be present in our sample galaxies with the given sensitivity. Our research finds that M 31 shows comparable radio-thermal emission to NGC 4736 but lacks the peak in emission usually linked with AME. Our research finds that M 31 shows excess emission beyond its expected emission. Our research finds that M 31 and NGC 4736 have the Far-infrared - Radio index

Ammonium sulfate's seemingly uncomplicated nature belies a significant ferroelectric phase transition accompanied by an exceptionally large entropy variation and both electrocaloric and barocaloric properties. To clarify the origins of these properties, we used $^{14}$N and $^{15}$N isotopic labeling, X-ray diffraction, and first-principles calculations to investigate the sulfate ion's breathing motion. Our study shows that sulfate ions are equally ordered on both sides during the transition and that the breathing motion significantly contributes to the entropy change. This work thus uncovered the complex framework of sulfate ion oscillations driving ammonium sulfate's ferroelectric and caloric behaviors.

In probabilistic learning, organisms sometimes opt for a less than optimal strategy known as probability-matching, which means choosing options based on their reward probabilities, as opposed to always choosing the best option, which is the optimal approach.  Despite being less efficient, probability-matching can be a viable option that works in the long run. A recent study suggests that a suboptimal strategy might be the most suitable choice for most cases, which would explain why humans often rely on it.  To investigate this possibility, researchers asked humans to play a long series of experiments, which included different versions of a classic reinforcement learning game.  To test whether the findings are natural and adaptive, they also collected data on people's choices when playing a series of experiments together.  Previous studies found that mistakes in choosing options are closely linked to the prediction error in the midbrain, which measures the difference between the participant's expectations and the actual reward.  To test the relationship between the suboptimal strategies and the midbrain activity, they also collected EEG data from the participants.  Interestingly, the data showed that the probability-matching strategy is the most natural and adaptive choice in these experiments, which means choosing options based on their reward probabilities, as opposed to always choosing the best option, which is the optimal approach.  To understand why this strategy might be the most natural and adaptive choice, they also tested a version of the game where the rewards are not consistent, which makes the optimal strategy less natural and adaptive,

A proposed Witting configuration, with a different complexity of 40 rays, could reformulate the Penrose model for spin-3/2 systems based on a dodecahedron's geometry, to study quantum mechanics' nonlocality and contextuality. An alternative setup using 120 states is examined in this work. Despite their different sizes, both arrangements share the same properties and have equivalent mathematical structures. An investigation into a more developed version of E8 root system is also presented, utilizing the 240-node complete graph K240. Two sets of states, defined by two different complexifications of E8, are used in this setup: one set using 40 nodes and another with 120 nodes, both sharing the same geometric structure. Interestingly, both configurations have equivalent mathematical structures despite their different sizes. It is shown that both setups have quantum mechanics' nonlocality and contextuality. An interpretation of these results in terms of E8 Lie algebra is presented and some interesting cohomological implications are revealed.

The continuous Fréchet distance c-approximate near neighbor problem involves precomputing a data structure that efficiently finds closest polygonal curves within a certain radius from query curves, considering an approximation factor for potential inaccuracies. This study primarily investigates this problem using time series curves, providing a comprehensive analysis for one-dimensional curves. By improving existing results, the research offers multiple tradeoffs between approximation quality, preprocessing efficiency, and query speed. Key outcomes include achieving the same performance as the previously best result for an improved approximation factor while also reaching the previously best result with reduced query complexity. Additionally, lower bounds on the data structure's efficiency were derived using the Orthogonal Range Search lower bounds, although not necessarily in straight line dimension.

To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current methods employ counteractive postprocessing techniques known as measurement error mitigation (MEM). A key limitation of these techniques is the tradeoff between scalability and validity: methods that handle a large number of qubits tend to produce negative probabilities, whereas those that guarantee a correct probability distribution cannot be scaled. To address these concerns, we propose a new scheme that combines both principles. Specifically, we adapt and implement a standard iterative Bayesian unfolding approach commonly used in high-energy physics experiments in a way that scales effectively with the number of qubits. Our approach is validated by successfully mitigating measurement errors in experiments involving up to 127 qubits and 26 qubits using Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger and Bernstein-Vazirani algorithms, respectively.

When humans operate robot arms, it is frequently assumed that the goal is to carry out tasks for the benefit of both humans and robots. However, when working in close proximity with humans, it is essential to consider not only task objectives but also any intentions and preferences the human may have. We suggest that a more beneficial method of shared human-robot collaboration involves recognizing and adapting to these underlying assumptions. In our research, we develop a shared autonomy paradigm where human instructions and robotic receptiveness are synchronized by adjusting transmission rates and key compression strategies. Participants achieved higher outcomes, fewer disruptions, and greater system productivity as a result of this approach.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, they require a detailed spatial understanding derived from self-generated and self-localized mapping processes. Current approaches mainly focus on metric localization and mapping, leaving an inherent gap in topological mapping for autonomous navigation. In this research, we present a hierarchical topological map representation known as HiTMap, which combines the advantages of self-localization, self-mapping, and topology-based navigation systems to enable autonomous navigation in unknown environments. The proposed HiTMap framework features an adaptive structure that reflects similar areas of operation and utilizes a metric map for localized mapping and a topology-based map representation, along with an self-localization system based on information filters. To facilitate navigation, HiTMap incorporates a connection-based controller that determines the next site to visit based on connections set within the topology map. The proposed HiTMap was thoroughly tested using both simulated and real-world data, and the results demonstrated its ability to generate and maintain topological maps while localizing within unknown environments. Furthermore, the system was found to successfully apply topology-based navigation for autonomous operation, with validation supported by experimental results from both indoor and outdoor environments.

Research into efficient two-dimensional linear space-time codes has significant interest in terms of avoiding interference in multiple paths. To this end, a new inter-group complementary code suite is introduced, consisting of multivariable functions, which can be viewed as a special type of 2-D linear space-time code. By selecting specific variables in multivariable functions, we obtain a comprehensive model for inter-group complementary code construction, offering a versatile approach. Moreover, a 2-D Z-complementary array code suite is constructed using multivariable functions, which has been proven to be optimal according to established criteria.

Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. Omitting these variations may result in image distortions such as beam hardening, which poses an additional challenge. In certain settings, the dual effects of radiation and electronic signal degradation caused by devices such as CCD cameras contribute to image degradation. A proposed variational reconstruction model leverages the characteristics of Poisson distribution, anisotropic diffusion, and principal component analysis (PCA), which effectively penalizes image gradients, separates signal components, and distinguishes between materials with distinct attenuation characteristics. Numerical simulations demonstrate improved image quality across various dimensions including 1-D, 2-D, and 3-D tomography.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unappealing results such as divergent fields and excessive energy losses. Notably, the desirable results obtained from the hydrodynamics model can also be achieved with a simple local approach that excludes the spillover and conventional Thomas-Fermi gap by introducing a modified Thomas-Fermi gap of approximately 0.135 eV.

In this research, we investigate the user's part in Contextual Named Entity Retrieval (CNER), revealing (1) that humans outperform automated methods in pinpointing context-sensitive terms, and (2) that enhanced results can be achieved when users also specify the relative significance of those terms. Although CNER bears some resemblance to related concepts such as List Question answering and Entity disambiguation, its primary goal is to gather user feedback to dynamically construct a class of entity profiles and leverage this data for extracting entities from unrestricted text. Our focus in CNER involves identifying relevant sentences containing entities similar to a selected query entity. This paper explores ways to gather human feedback and assign importance weights in CNER, enhancing its overall performance. Our findings are grounded in experiments conducted with both IR researchers and a pool of crowdsourced workers.

Time-based data refers to information measured against the backdrop of time, giving it a distinct structural context that forms the foundation of its constituent parts. When dealing with multi-variable data sets that change over time, we anticipate observing interconnected patterns, long-term fluctuations, seasonal variations, and correlations across different variables. In contrast, longitudinal data often displays relationships between and within individual units over time, including both intra- and inter-subject correlations. While analyzing time series and longitudinal data differs in certain aspects, they frequently employ similar visual display methods. Our approach focuses on creating an interactive framework that allows users to explore and dissect the time-based components of these data types, including how to transform and manipulate the data. Given that temporal data often intersects with other forms of data, we also outline methods for seamlessly linking time-based visualizations with other data displays. The proposed concepts are formalized into a structured data processing pipeline and translated into a comprehensive R package, cranvas, which provides users with a diverse array of interactive graphics designed to facilitate comprehensive data exploration and diagnostics.

The promising potential of extracting useful insights from Electronic Health Records (EHRs) has emerged as a crucial area of study, as machine learning models can assist healthcare professionals in decision-making to enhance overall healthcare quality. Advances in recent years have seen the development of new EHR-based tasks using sequential or graph-based models, as well as inspired graph neural networks (GNNs). Despite their achievements, existing solutions often overlook the diversity of EHR data by treating various components as part of a unified structure. This often leads to diminished performance when dealing with the complex relationships present in EHR big data. To address these shortcomings, we introduce HSGNN, a novel hybrid model that leverages GNNs and supports the creation of diverse and adaptable neighborhood structures for EHR data. This allows for the accurate representation of data's geometric and topological properties, as well as the exploration of implicit connections within EHR big data. The implementation of our method is carried out using a heterogeneous similarity graph, as well as various designed neighborhood learning schemes to extract meaningful structural information from EHR data. Ultimately, we conduct thorough experiments on three new datasets to validate our approach's efficacy, as its applications achieve state-of-the-art results across different EHR-based EOD tasks.

Using a mean-field approach and considering both non-uniform particle sizes and solvent effects, we model the behavior of the electric double layer at the boundary of a charged flexible material. From a free energy model, we calculate the electrostatic potential and number of water and ions within the boundary using coupled differential equations, including the Poisson equation. We discover that solvent effects profoundly impact the electrostatic potential, ion counts, and permittivity of the electrolyte near the boundary of the charged flexible material. Furthermore, we learn that taking solvent effects into account intensifies the Donnan potential and demonstrates that within the boundary of sufficiently small charged particles, the hyperbolic relationship between ion counts and applied potential holds. However, for larger sizes, the relationship shifts from hyperbolic to a saturation point. Lastly, we observe that the model permits a continuous transition from the Gouy-Chapman to the Grahame model.

Automating the labor-intensive and error-prone process of extracting requirements from unstructured text is a highly recommended goal for many researchers. To this end, we annotated a unique dataset, PURE, and derived a new one combining requirements and non-requirements. We refined a BERT model with this dataset and compared its outcomes with those of traditional machine learning algorithms. To evaluate the model's performance, we used six distinct metrics across five distinct datasets, observing that the BERT model consistently excelled at these measurements. We further tailored the model to adapt to varying text types and tested its applicability to real-world extracts from actual project documentation, assessing its performance on pure requirement texts. The model's source code, dataset, and documentation can be accessed at https://github.com/fatemehkarimii/PURE.

This research investigates the energy efficiency in a multi-user, multi-relay communication system with a maximum diversity network coding technique. A direct link is available between the source and destination for each user, and they can choose between using this direct link or a network coded relay path for better performance. By combining relay scheduling and transmitter power adaptation, optimal performance is achieved, focusing on minimizing energy consumption while maintaining a specified output bit rate. This problem is shown to have a mathematical optimization solution but due to its computational complexity, an approximate method is suggested, using a multi-agent iterative optimization algorithm. Our results show that this approach significantly outperforms traditional methods for performance and energy efficiency.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local density of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results were compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in experimental spectra was explained by suggesting that it corresponds to a small $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state or by attributing it to a YSR state formed by an s-d interaction between a Mn impurity and a Nb surface atom. Furthermore, by applying the theoretical framework to an S=2 Mn dimer, a YSR state with a distinct character was identified in the experimental spectrum, and the spectral positions, splitting patterns, and relative intensities of the YSR states were accurately predicted. This theoretical framework provides an adaptable model for analyzing and interpreting experimental data in a wide range of superconductor/impurity systems.

Techniques such as the Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) can efficiently register and accurately bound point cloud errors for scenes without moving objects.  However, traditional methods struggle in scenes where there are changes in view.  To improve point cloud registration for dynamic scenes, deep learning-based approaches have shown potential.  Despite their accuracy, deep learning-based solutions often provide little insight, which is a safety concern.  To balance these needs, our paper introduces an approach that involves selectively removing portions of the point cloud with inconsistencies, using local network estimates to identify potential registration errors and validate registration accuracy across entire point clouds.  To enhance our method's efficiency, our approach leverages the invariant U-Net architecture and accelerates point processing through optimized sampling methods.  The proposed method achieves accurate registration, provides thorough validation, and significantly improves processing efficiency.  We demonstrate our approach's effectiveness by applying it to various dynamic scenes using 2D and 3D point clouds.

Satellite images are widely employed across multiple sectors, encompassing 
agriculture, navigation, and urban planning, often resulting in immense 
databases requiring extensive computational power for processing. Deep 
learning methods have recently gained traction for satellite image analysis. 
Although these methods offer excellent performance, they necessitate substantial 
compute power and pose challenges for broad adoption, particularly in scenarios 
where high-powered infrastructure is lacking. This paper presents a new edge 
detection technique that utilizes deep learning but operates efficiently on lower 
end hardware due to its limited memory and processing speed advantages. The 
approach is evaluated using the Edget4imge benchmark, which compares our 
method's performance to current state-of-the-art techniques.

Subjecting solid materials to an ultra-intense, femtosecond X-ray pulse from a free-electron laser causes drastic electronic excitation, triggering a complex series of valence and core electron dynamics. The process involves processes driven by electron-phonon and electron-electron interactions, leading to phenomena like exciton effects, Mott absorption, and near-edge resonance in liquid and solid materials. Researchers have developed a model that describes the interplay of valence and core electrons to predict these effects, incorporating interactions that form excitons at high densities around the Fermi level. The model has been applied to the X-ray absorption near edge spectra of liquid and solid carbon, showing that its predictions align well with the experimental spectra, especially concerning the energy shift associated with liquid carbon's excitation. The efficiency and relative simplicity of this model make it a valuable tool for analyzing and understanding the excitonic effects and changes driven by core electron excitation at megahertz to petahertz timescales in solid materials, as well as core-excited resonances in both liquid and solid materials surrounding the 1s absorption peak.

The application of a Deep Neural Network in Automatic Modulation Classification (AMC) exhibits enhanced performance compared to traditional methods even in harsh wireless environments; nonetheless, such networks can be vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This research proposes an effective solution to counter and explore such vulnerabilities within AMC DNNs by employing a Resilience Mixture GAN (RM-GAN) to generate protective adversarial examples. The suggested robust DNN architecture is based on a mixture model, allowing for the learning and representation of a complex distribution formed by mixtures of multiple non-Gaussian distributions, which in turn aids in learning the input space classification model of a AMC DNN. This structure can also synthesize defensive examples that counteract malicious attacks, enabling a reliable and secure AMC service over wireless channels. This research uses data from two wireless channels, HPA and Rician, with diverse scattering environments, to demonstrate its efficacy.

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is an issue that experts struggle with,
especially when interpreting MRI scans. Given that clinical data continuously
flows in from multiple sources, hospitals struggle to find an effective approach
to achieve consistent results. We investigated how continuous learning can be
applied to a real-world medical problem by fine-tuning a deep learning model
initially trained on a large reference dataset of 3000 patients, and then
expanding its capabilities to datasets from three additional hospitals combined.
We compare performance not only of the models themselves, but also of experts
and non-experts, as well as analyzing how lesion types, hospital size, and data
quantity impact the models' performance. We found that a model trained on a
reference dataset and then extended with datasets from five hospitals, all of
which had significantly fewer patients than the initial reference dataset, and
thus offered relatively limited information, exhibited good performance. Even
when the additional information consisted of datasets with a higher proportion
of lesions than the reference dataset, the model's performance remained stable.
In contrast, a model trained from scratch directly using the combined datasets
without initial training from the reference dataset, did not match the
performance of the previously trained model. Therefore, extending a well-
performing reference dataset to incorporate new, but smaller datasets from
other hospitals can effectively support long-term decision-making in clinical
settings. We discuss the practical implications of these findings and suggest
