A novel type of metric comparison analogous to Alexandrov comparison is established, 
and its relationship to optimal transport between measures on a Riemannian manifold 
is demonstrated, specifically with respect to the MTW condition proposed by Xi-Nan 
Ma, Neil Trudinger and Xu-Jia Wang, involving geodesic balls with non-negative curvature.

Across various disciplines, there's considerable interest in creating predictive models for complex systems using data. To tackle this, we've developed an innovative framework that learns the discrepancies between a dynamical system and its predictions. This framework can operate with or without prior knowledge of the system's dynamics, relying on differential equations or machine-learning based approaches. We've demonstrated its effectiveness through numerical experiments using two contrasting datasets from fluid mechanics, showing the original model's improvements and other desirable properties. This framework provides a versatile platform (available at https://github.com/axjgul/lemo) for exploring the potential of data-driven, collaborative learning, which could lead to enhanced models and a deeper understanding of the system's underlying dynamics.

A statistical analysis identified two cores within the Dragon Infrared Dark Cloud exhibiting an increase in mass through the accumulation of surrounding material. Utilizing a kinematic model of the cloud, it was found that one core located at R$_{DC}$\,250 exhibits changes over time from 2011 to 2018, while another core at R$_{DC}$\,350 has shown changes from 2011 to2015 to 2018. Data collected from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array revealed the cores maintain a centered velocity. Moreover, velocity profiles indicate the cores rotate about their centers at the pace of 1.5 to 2.5\,km\,s$^{-1}$ over a 20-second period. The measured motions can be described as orderly, characteristic of stars in the early stages of formation. The cores' growth spans at least three years, corresponding to a significant increase in mass by a factor of three, suggesting the protostars possess sufficient energy to drive the surrounding material. The protostars' masses range between 1.5 and 2.5 times that of our sun and it is likely they will develop into massive stars, potentially two to three times the mass of our sun. The evolution of these cores implies the formation of massive stars within the cloud is likely. The protostars' location near the cloud's rotation axis, close to a filament axis, may play a role in suppressing turbulence. The observed

The theoretical primordial black holes that form in the universe are offered as a possible explanation for dark matter. Variations in these black holes, depending on how they are formed and their actual existence, can have notable effects on cosmic phenomena, making them a topic that researchers study actively. Determining the statistical properties of these black holes, especially their mass distribution, is crucial in understanding their role in the universe. An advanced, high-performance algorithm called PopSyCLE has been used to study the statistical properties of these black holes in multiple cosmological scenarios. Our work extends PopSyCLE to also account for the influence of primordial black holes on the universe. We provide results on the mass function, number density, and clustering properties of these black holes for various formation scenarios. These black holes can potentially leave noticeable imprints on the universe' large-scale structure, offering a unique way to verify the theory that these black holes constitute dark matter. Furthermore, our predictions can guide observations and experiments related to these black holes, such as their potential role in gravitational wave events.

We conducted research into systems at equilibrium consisting of uniform wedge-shaped molecules using Monte Carlo simulations, where each molecule consisted of six aligned spheres of gradually decreasing sizes, and the shape of these molecules was defined solely by the ratio of the smallest to the largest sphere diameters, referred to as parameter $d$. The systems' phases were studied as a function of parameter $d$ and the packing density of molecules $\eta$, under the condition that only repulsive interactions were present. This led to the system's behavior being controlled solely by the entropy of molecular arrangement. For systems where the packing density was below $0.5$, in addition to the standard liquid state, we observed standard nematic and smectic A liquid crystalline phases. Conversely, when the packing density exceeded $0.5$, two distinct polar crystalline phases emerged alongside the nematic and smectic A liquid crystalline phases, depending on the value of parameter $d$. One of these polar crystalline phases was characterized by the uniform alignment of its molecular director and featured specific arrangements of the smallest and largest spheres within the molecule, known as the $A_{1a}$ phase. The other polar crystalline phase, known as the $A_{3a}$ phase in accordance with its third-order splay elasticity, did not exhibit this uniformity and featured oblique arrangements of its molecular directors and the offset $3/2$ arrangement of the smallest and largest spheres. This unique $A_{3a}$ phase was found

Our goal with parameter-efficient tuning is to minimize updates to model parameters
when adapting a pre-trained model to downstream tasks. This paper proposes PASTA,
where we adjust only the special token embeddings, like separator and classification tokens in BERT, just before self-attention operations in each Transformer layer.
By doing this, PASTA can achieve performance on par with fine-tuning for natural language understanding tasks like text categorization and named entity recognition while updating a mere 0.029% of all parameters.
Our contribution offers a straightforward yet efficient way to fine-tune models, with applications across various deployment scenarios for pre-trained language models.

This paper investigates a complex problem where we need to assess the impact of adding items to a collection. The inherent nature of this problem prevents us from making absolute preferences between options since adding an item to a subset is a distinct action from adding it to another subset, even if the subsets contain the same items. To tackle this issue, we analyzed two approaches: one relying on contextual preferences, generating preferences between specific additions, and another grounded in non-contextual preferences, ranking entire sets for comparison. The use of contextual preferences has the advantage of considering a broader range of additions, but the non-contextual approach can provide preferences for any subset versus another, a more common query type. Inspired by these insights, we devised two algorithms. The first is based on a constraint generation approach, aiming to find an optimal list of preferences through simulated debates between sets. The second algorithm uses a beam search strategy to identify a balanced list of preferences at a intermediate level of specificity. Experimental results showed that both algorithms performed well, achieving high accuracy, coverage, and compliance. Moreover, the algorithms' results demonstrated a fine-tuned trade-off between making strong and weak preferences, which could be manipulated via a beam size parameter. Ultimately, the beam search algorithm yielded an enriched context with more options, but at the cost of less complete preference lists compared to the constraint generation algorithm.

Our application of the lattice cluster theory for polymer fluids has established that the configurational entropy, enthalpy, and internal energy are interconnected thermodynamic properties as supported by recent experimental data from Caruthers and Medvedev. This relationship enables us to reframe the generalized entropy theory for glass formation, combining the lattice cluster theory and Adam-Gibbs model, based on any of these properties to simplify the analysis. By utilizing thermodynamic scaling to assess correlations between properties and dynamics, we identified key thermodynamic characteristics related to dynamics and investigated the origin of this scaling through direct comparisons and theoretical modeling of structural correlations. The thermodynamic scaling was found to be a general phenomenon regardless of the specific enthalpy or internal energy model used, while the choice of entropy basis affects the specific correlations observed. The primary advantage of this approach lies in its ability to resolve discrepancies between thermodynamic and dynamic measurements and to improve accuracy in enthalpy or internal energy modeling. Furthermore, this method facilitates a clearer connection between the thermodynamics of slow relaxation and the kinetics of structural changes in glass-forming polymer fluids.

Transformer-based language models have been shown to struggle with logical reasoning, especially when it involves negation. Unlike previous studies that relied on psycholinguistic tools, our research delves into types of negation from developmental psychology. We examine this knowledge gap through a natural language inference task by creating a set of specialized questions from existing NLI datasets, which helps us assess a range of models' ability to process these negation types. Our analysis indicates models perform notably well on some negation categories, revealing a significant distinction in their handling of this concept.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This paper examines the interdependence of target words and proposes a novel look-ahead attention mechanism that allows direct sourcing of information from target words generated further ahead. We demonstrate that integrating this mechanism into conventional attention models leads to significant enhancements in both translation quality and target word accuracy, especially for state-of-the-art transformer models. Experimental results show substantial improvements over a wide range of translation benchmarks.

We propose a method to calculate the Kontsevich weights for the graphs of connection and curvature in the context of symplectic Poisson structures. This weight has practical implications, especially for determining the symplectic symmetries of the Drinfeld-Sokolov connection and the symplectic form on the symplectic Yang-Mills quantum field theory's space. Consequently, our weights will be used to compute the symplectic form on the moduli space of monodromy representations of symplectic Nambu-Poisson connections. Furthermore, our findings provide insight into the symplectic structure on the moduli space of symplectic Nambu-Poisson structures.

This research involves determining the large N limit of $O(N)$ models with non-polynomial potential functions in odd dimensional spaces, leading to a new class of interacting conformal field theories. Specifically, these models have complex coefficients in their perturbation expansions. A study of their thermal entropy in two and three dimensions reveals non-standard behavior distinct from the holographic c-entropy, mirroring a similar discrepancy in entanglement entropy observed in $2+1$ dimensions. In contrast to the holographic c-entropy, these non-standard entropies do not exhibit convexity. To facilitate computational efficiency, this research relies on a simple new method for calculating renormalized entropies. Moreover, the entanglement entropy in $2+1$ and $3+1$ dimensions exhibits similar non-standard behavior, while convexity is retained in $1+1$ dimension due to a principle of analyticity.

Cai, Song and Kou published a paper in 2013 that introduced a method for pricing Asian options using a combination of a class of constant fields within a mathematical framework, known as CF-AF. The CF-AF method, outlined in their work, provided a way to calculate the price of such options by approximating a mathematical solution. The paper also referred to a separate, previously published article by Li and Yuen in 2009, which AF claimed to have incorporated elements of. The correct interpretation, however, revealed that CF-AF represents a distinct method that uses a separate, unrelated approach known as the CZL method, developed by Chen, Song and Yang. The CF-AF method itself suffered from a number of issues including incorrect results, poor convergence and an overly broad definition. The AF paper also contained inaccuracies in regards to the application of a separate method known as the GA method, developed by Glasserman and Wang, which had not been mentioned in the original publication. Finally, a separate method known as the LA method had been referenced incorrectly as having been discussed in a particular conference, when in fact it had not been part of that conference.

The source behind the diffuse gamma-ray background is currently unknown. However, various galactic features such as star-forming and starburst galaxies, black holes, and cosmic clusters may all play a part in this phenomenon. Researchers conducted a study that simulated how cosmic rays interact within galactic clusters using cosmological magnetohydrodynamical models. Their analysis, spanning a range of redshift values, suggests that clusters of galaxies could account for up to 100 percent of the gamma-ray flux measured by Fermi-LAT at energy levels above 100 GeV, assuming certain conditions are met. Specifically, these conditions include specific spectral indices and energy cutoffs, and clusters of a certain mass and redshift. Their predictions also anticipate future observations of high-energy gamma-rays from clusters using upcoming experiments like HAWC and CTA.

Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. This prospect expands the scope of cosmological collider physics, where the signals produced by these particles are usually suppressed by the Boltzmann distribution. Our analysis explores the mechanics of a cosmic collider through two types of primordial features. Firstly, we consider oscillating primordial features, encompassing cases of massive field oscillations and oscillatory features in the inflationary potential. Secondly, we look at any sharp feature within an inflationary model. These features can induce unsuppressed quantum fluctuations in heavy fields, leaving detectable signatures in primordial non-Gaussian patterns, and revealing details about the spectra of these heavy degrees of freedom.

Understanding how complex visual models work is crucial, and developing techniques to explain these models can be particularly challenging. To address this issue, a framework called LaViSE is proposed to enable convolutional neural networks to describe their internal workings in plain text. By using generic image data, this approach creates a link between visual and semantic information, allowing for its application across different domains without explicit labels. The LaViSE framework has a flexible structure, making it possible to analyze any network, regardless of whether its training data is accessible. Moreover, this technique can produce new explanations that go beyond the categories initially learned during training. It also has a significant application in discovering biases within datasets without needing additional labels. To facilitate further research, the framework, datasets, and code are openly available.

Developing a simplified microscopic model of cuprates is crucial in uncovering the mechanism behind high-temperature superconductivity. By comparing the interaction between adjacent and non-adjacent electrons within a doped edge-sharing two-dimensional cuprate, we observe that adjacent electrons exhibit repulsive forces, whereas non-adjacent electrons show attractive forces mediated by phonons. We have also determined that coupling between electrons in different dimensions can drive the formation of Cooper pairs in one-dimensional systems. Consequently, high temperatures can maintain the stability of these pairs due to the decreasing effect of phonons. Notably, it's feasible to adjust the parameters of our model so that the attractive forces between non-adjacent electrons surpass those between adjacent ones. Ultimately, our research suggests that one-dimensional systems of strongly coupled edge-sharing dimer electrons may offer a valuable framework for exploring the microscopic processes behind high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates.

The ongoing Population-based HIV Impact Assessment project aims to measure national and regional progress in combating the HIV epidemic, a primary goal of UNAIDS' 90-90-90 targets. By analyzing data from high-risk countries in sub-Saharan Africa, researchers hope to gain a deeper understanding of the key factors driving the epidemic. This study focuses on six countries - Burundi, Haiti, Kenya, Malawi, Rwanda, and Tanzania - and explores the potential benefits of utilizing causal machine learning algorithms to identify crucial indicators for targeting HIV interventions. By employing a causal structural learning algorithm on the Malawi Individual Data Set, the study's findings illustrate the capabilities of causal structural learning in uncovering important relationships in epidemiological research and guiding intervention strategies to achieve the UNAIDS 90-90-90 targets.

In the chiral magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ of $\beta$-Mn type, it's discovered that the transition from a metastable skyrmion lattice at room temperature to an unstable state goes through a temporary stage of topological melting. This phase transition, which was not seen in other materials of similar structure, is attributed to the unique stability of the skyrmion lattice and the weak stability of the magnetization in Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$. A theoretical model that takes into account the skyrmion's energy density explains this phenomenon and predicts that skyrmion-mass-like effects will arise in this system. Finally, it's been demonstrated that the stability of the skyrmion lattice can be enhanced by applying a magnetic field of several kiloOersted.

High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor Models are thoroughly explored, covering key 
assumptions and their underlying rationales, significant outcomes, and example
exhibits through simple demonstrations. The theory and implementation of 
these models, focusing specifically on singular ARMA models, is examined. The 
survey emphasizes practical implications and technological aspects of these 
models, highlighting both the state-of-the-art research and the areas where 
further investigation is required.

The equilibrium problem described by the Nikaid\^o-Isoda-Fan inequality encompasses several key problems like optimization, variational inequality, and others, as specific instances. This paper aims to provide a clear outline illustrating the connection between fixed points of the Moreau proximal mapping and solutions to the equilibrium problem that satisfy particular monotonicity and Lipschitz-type constraints.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. Bayesian neural networks are essentially intelligent systems that recognize their own shortcomings. To accurately quantify uncertainty, we incorporate a predictive likelihood assessment tool. Experimentation reveals that BNNs exhibit lower overall error rates compared to traditional predictive models. Moreover, our novel approach demonstrates enhanced steganographic capacity as it effectively measures its own uncertainty.

The debate on turbulent effects influencing magnetic activity in the Sun and stars persists. Investigating this phenomenon is a complex task, made easier by analytical mean-field models that simplify the dynamics and offer insights into the underlying physics. Our study utilizes a global mean-field dynamo model to simulate the magnetic activity in mean-field dynamos, and through this, we observe the effects produced by turbulent fields on the results. In particular, we've discovered that considering higher-order turbulent effects is essential for accurate representation, and neglecting them might lead to incorrect inferences about the dynamos' characteristics. Our findings validate the concept of reverse averaging, allowing us to isolate and analyze the impact of turbulent effects. Our research shows that turbulent effects based on the mean-field modeling framework influence magnetic energy, and reverse averaging helps to identify the most significant effects. Additionally, we've created tables to simplify the calculation of crucial parameters for mean-field dynamos, and our work offers evidence for an alternative explanation of magnetic activity cycles, and offers a deeper understanding of dynamos in the Sun and stars.

A study has revealed molecular outflows in the central area of the galaxy NGC4945 using the ALMA. At a high resolution of ~0.3", the ALMA detected four distinct plumes of molecular gas, possibly corresponding to gas situated at the edges of an existing ionized outflow. Observations of line-of-sight velocities exceeding 450 km/s indicate outflow velocities exceeding 600 km/s in the fastest emitting plume. Most of these molecular gas outflows have counterparts in the emissions of HCN and HCO+. A proposed model suggests the molecular gas outflows have a cone-like geometry similar to ionized outflows and share the galaxy's rotation velocity when expelled. Using this model, it's possible to calculate the speed of ejected material and account for unobserved outflows due to confusion with the galaxy's disk. It's also possible that some of the emissions are due to standing waves from cloud-like clumps of molecular gas. At an assumed distance of 3.13 kpc, the study found that molecular gas expelling amounts to 0.6-2.9 solar masses per second. In the context of galaxy evolution, the amount of molecular gas lost may be a key factor.

A simplified version of the original Vlasov-Maxwell equations for magnetized plasmas is provided by quasilinear theory, describing how particles interact with waves through resonant processes. The reduced model in a turbulent regime shows that the distribution of particles changes over time due to a kinetic diffusion effect, where the rate of change is influenced by the density of wave energy. The model also predicts that the density of wave energy in a given spectral space evolves according to a reaction equation, with the rate of growth dependent on the distribution of particles. A numerical approach, the conservative Galerkin method, is proposed for the quasilinear model in both momentum space and spectral space. The approach ensures the preservation of physical conservation laws, employing conservative discrete equations and a corresponding quadrature method. A semi-implicit time evolution is also implemented to efficiently solve the quasilinear model. The numerical method's effectiveness is demonstrated through numerical experiments for both the linear and nonlinear regimes, with the results accurately predicting the long-term statistical behavior of the Vlasov-Maxwell equations.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis.

We provide a relationship between the exponential stability of a C0-semigroup T and solutions of a specific Lyapunov inequality in B+(X,X*), where X is a Banach space. The inequality's solutions determine the boundedness of the resolvent R(λ,A) inside and outside the left half-plane and left invertibility of T, the C0-semigroup.

This paper introduces MuMuPy, a computational software and web-based tool for determining the interaction cross sections between dimuonium (true muonium) and matter, also computing corresponding form factors. With MuMuPy, users can estimate the likelihood of dimuonium transitioning within an atomic nucleus' electric field. Developed with the muon-based muon-muon electron-positron collider, the muon-muon electron collider, a low-energy electron collider, project proposed by our institute, the Institute of Nuclear Physics at the Budker Institute. We tested the reliability of MuMuPy against prior research results for a range of inputs.

Portfolio managers assess investment success in relation to market standards, specifically using the Standard & Poor 500 index as a benchmark. Our revised assessment combines two key measures: the portfolio's absolute value and its performance relative to that of a chosen benchmark. The traditional Merton problem, in which an investor seeks to maximize utility through portfolio returns, is first adapted to accommodate both absolute and relative wealth in a scenario where the benchmark's value remains unknown. The patient investor's decision-making process is then modeled after a power utility function, and it is discovered that an optimal strategy involves holding all assets in the portfolio equity market. Next, we explore a scenario where an investor can choose multiple benchmark stocks. The uncertainty surrounding the benchmark's performance makes it necessary to find an optimal strategy that balances risk and reward, using a different method each time. Ultimately, we demonstrate that an optimal strategy exists and can be calculated analytically, and through numerical examples, we illustrate how varying utility parameters affects this outcome, resulting in a diverse assortment of optimal strategies.

The most abundant galaxy type in the cosmos is dwarf galaxies, which exhibit distinct characteristics when compared to larger, brighter counterparts. This article centers on the physical and chemical properties of the interstellar material within dwarf galaxies containing notable quantities of gas and dust. The discussion includes the characteristics of neutral and ionized gases, the effects of dust, and initial evidence suggesting the presence of active nuclei in these galaxies. The article also considers the cosmological implications of primordial helium abundance and the similarity between local Green Pea galaxies and younger, proto-galactic systems in the early universe.

We examine the stability of fermionic quasiparticles in a fermion-boson model based on a Bethe lattice, where fermions interact with local bosons through a Peierls coupling. By reducing the complex model into a non-interacting chain with varying site potentials, we demonstrate that despite the presence of multiple bosonic excitations costing zero energy, the quasiparticle remains robustly stable for large boson couplings. However, the quasiparticle's stability is reduced as the couplings approach zero, resulting in an increase in the density of states at the Fermi level and the emergence of localized bosonic states. Furthermore, the collapse of the quasiparticle is characterized by an anomalous decrease in its self-energy, which can be attributed to an unusual phenomenon: the rare collapse occurs through the simultaneous disappearance of multiple quasiparticles instead of a single, localized bosonic state. We derive phase diagrams that describe the system's behavior based on the ratio of couplings and the presence of local bosonic states. Two distinct phases are observed: in the first, the system's quasiparticles remain robustly stable; in the second, the system's quasiparticles collapse through an increase in the system's self-energy and the emergence of multiple quasiparticles rather than a single localized bosonic state. Golan and Sapir \cite{MR3978542} showed that the Thompson's groups $F$, $T$, and $V$ exhibit linear divergence. The present work extends this analysis to broader classes of these groups. Specifically, we investigate the Brown-Thompson groups $F_n$, $T_n$, and $V_n$ and discover that they too have a linear divergence function. Furthermore, our research encompasses the braided Thompson groups $BF$, $\widehat{BF}$, and $\widehat{BV}$. Alongside existing results in \cite{Kodama:2020to}, our findings confirm that these braided groups display linear divergence as well.

This paper demonstrates the end-to-end fine-tuning of the Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture. Key technical hurdles are identified that must be overcome to accomplish this goal. A comparative analysis is performed of RAG configurations using different pre-trained models, including both ELSA and Deliberate, as well as various combinations of science and PMI retrievers. Our results indicate that the Deliberate configuration outperforms others on SciAIL-1. We contend that successfully end-to-end fine-tuning the RAG architecture for question answering is a critical benchmark, similar to fine-tuning BERT, and hope this work inspires the development of more architectures that can be fully fine-tuned for a broad range of NLP tasks.

This study calculates the long-term behavior of the recurrence coefficients for polynomials that are orthogonal in relation to a specific logarithmic weight given by $\log\left(\frac{2k}{1-x}\right)$ over the interval $(-1,1)$ where $k>1$, and we verify a long-standing conjecture of A. Magnus regarding these coefficients, making use of the Riemann-Hilbert and steepest descent methods in an unconventional manner since no solution to the related problem near the singular point at $x=1$ exists in the current mathematical literature.

Utilizing crowdsourcing platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk to acquire top-tier human annotations proves more complicated than initially thought, influenced by several key factors, such as task instructions and annotator compensation, among others. To prevent inaccurate annotations which could mislead automatic summarization systems, we develop a multi-stage recruitment process targeting high-quality MTurk workers. By establishing demographic filters and incorporating detailed task descriptions, along with a straightforward annotation task, we effectively recruit an ensemble of skilled annotators. Subsequently, we introduce an innovative salary run mechanism to ensure the assembly of a diverse pool of annotators, leveraging their prior engagement in relevant work. Ultimately, our strategy enables the retrieval of a set of experienced and trustworthy MTurk workers, yielding numerous accurate annotations while minimizing the expense associated with their acquisition.

Text-video retrieval, an essential task of practical importance, has seen escalating interest, with the focus on crafting nuanced spatial-temporal video representations being a major research priority. Current state-of-the-art models for text-video retrieval primarily utilize pre-trained vision backbones with rigid network architectures, thereby hindering the ability to further refine the video representation and yielding suboptimal results. To overcome this limitation, we present TS2-Net, a groundbreaking transformer architecture incorporating dynamic token shifting and selection, which effectively tailors token sequences to capture the intricate movements in videos and pinpoint critical spatial and temporal details. The TS2-Net's adaptability in shifting token features across frames preserves comprehensive token information, and its token selection mechanism efficiently isolates semantically vital tokens from input videos. Thoroughly evaluating TS2-Net on major text-video retrieval benchmarks yields exceptional outcomes, with our method setting new records on MSRVTT, VATEX, LSMDC, ActivityNet, and DiDeMo.

We've found that neutral flavour-changing currents in the top sector are a natural extension of any theory that has $SU(2)L\otimes SU(2)R$ symmetries. Our approach enables us to calculate constraints on these symmetries at being less than the electroweak scale. We've found specific limits on the symmetry scale to be around 10-17 TeV, which is based on observations of top spin asymmetries in proton collisions. Furthermore, within this framework it is natural to explain the flavour paradigm by making all second generation right-handed quarks massive, thereby accounting for the small CKM elements. This approach also provides a mechanism for generating oblique correction parameters outside their standard range. Their values could significantly impact the possibility of having leptonic W decay.

In response to the intricacies of network data, a new type of hybrid network is suggested by combining rules for preferential attachment and uniform attachment.  A hybrid network created through this method begins with a core of attached nodes and then adds new nodes, directing a fraction α to attach to existing nodes in proportion to their degree and directing (1-α) to attach uniformly without any preferences.  Three scenarios for the uniform attachment scenario are explored: uniform attachment to the existing portfolio of degrees, uniform attachment proportional to the number of existing nodes, and a scenario-specific attachment that includes edgemanagement. A hybrid network created through this method with a given value of α for a large number of iterations |I| displays properties of both degree distributions from pure preferential attachment and uniform attachment scenarios, resulting in degenerate (zero) density functions. However, for all three scenarios for the uniform attachment, it is observed that the mean degree in a hybrid network grows according to a specific equation. Moreover, it is also shown that for scenario-specific attachment to the existing portfolio of attached degrees, it is possible to control the degeneracy and obtain a Gaussian-like degree distribution with a mean that grows according to a specific equation. Similarly, for scenario-specific attachment to both existing degrees and nodes, it is possible to obtain a Gaussian-like degree distribution with a mean that grows according to a specific equation. The expanding utilization of unlicensed frequency bands necessitates dependable interference management systems and hence reliable identification of wireless interference (WII). Our research proposes a novel WII technique based on multi-label classification, enabling real-time detection of multiple coexisting signals without requiring prior knowledge of signal patterns or frequencies. The method relies on a convolutional neural network (CNN) that analyzes spectrum readings, thereby reducing computation and memory demands compared to traditional signal processing approaches. Using CNN, WII can accurately detect multiple frequencies with sample rates as low as 155.52 kHz and minimum signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 10 dB within 80ms. The method achieves an accuracy of nearly 95% when detecting 15 to 25 frequency channels, surpassing existing approaches.

To grasp the impact of gravitational forces on both quantum systems moving at varying speeds and stationary systems, we must rely on accurate quantum mechanics theories. This project involves rectifying the inaccuracies in existing quantum mechanics theories for a cosmic string background, which had overlooked essential factors such as gravitational force effects on quantum systems with space and spin, the impact of gravitational force on quantum systems with space and spin, the impact of gravitational force on quantum systems with space and charge, and systems stationary in a gravitational field with a cosmic string. This project aims to develop a new quantum mechanics theory for these systems, which has been achieved through the established method of quantum mechanics. The relationship between energy and rotational frequency has been established for these systems, and a mathematical formula to calculate rotational frequency has been derived. The study shows that gravitational force and a cosmic string have significant effects on both stationary and moving systems, which allows us to develop a new quantum mechanics theory for these systems based on the established method of quantum mechanics.
Countable, locally standard measure algebras are parameterized by a pair of Steinitz numbers, consisting of one value which equals or exceeds 1.

Parton distributions that account for quark and gluon correlations in a proton can be understood by analyzing specific interactions between a proton and a photon, specifically in a process known as leptoproduction. Researchers in the field of Davis-Velasco-Cisquillo Leptoproduction aim to understand this interaction by studying its various phases, with an particular focus on the differential phase shift phenomenon to uncover information on the structure functions of a proton and its connections with the parton distributions that researchers are trying to understand. One of the goals of this research is to analyze the, previously unseen, reaction where the proton recoils with polarization in an experiment called CLAS, to be conducted at Jefferson Lab, and how this specific reaction can help scientists understand a proton's structure functions that are not known yet.

All AI systems inevitably make mistakes, characterized by their unpredictability and distinctness from human errors. A critical objective is to rectify these AI errors without compromising their established abilities and ideally without requiring direct human intervention. This report outlines an innovative approach aimed at boosting the cognitive capabilities of individual AI systems by collaborating with other AIs. It synthesizes insights from multi-agent learning systems and introduces novel mathematical techniques for non-recursive error correction. This research develops a foundational framework for advanced AI intelligence and explores its theoretical and practical implications through the analysis of concrete examples. These findings serve as a starting point for the practical application of this concept in diverse real-world domains.

Our research involves exploring the thermal behavior of the Bose-Hubbard model in the presence of strong spin-orbit coupling originating from a mean-field state. By introducing a spin-orbit coupling factor, $\lambda$, along with the inter- and intra-band hopping coefficients, $t_{\perp}$ and $t \parallel$, we examine how $\lambda$ impacts the phase diagram. Specifically, at low $\lambda$, the system exhibits insulating and superfluid phases separate by a topological transition at $\lambda_t = 0.30$. As $\lambda$ exceeds $\lambda_t$, the system enters a topological superfluid phase where the superfluid transition temperature decreases with increasing $\lambda$. Additionally, temperature-dependent studies for other key parameters such as critical temperature, transition shape, and heat capacity have been conducted to characterize these thermal phase transitions. Furthermore, at elevated $\lambda$, the system displays an expansion of its superfluid phase at high temperatures, accompanied by a shift in its critical temperature curve, ultimately peaking at $\lambda = 1.0$.

Consider two groups, G_1 and G_2, and suppose a homomorphism \phi from G_1 to G_2 maps a particular element to another element. In the context of graph theory, this leads to the concept of a group G_1 degrading to group G_2, which is also referred to as G_1 being degenerate with respect to G_2. Now, graphs are assigned to the groups based on how they can be embedded within a vector space with a specific dimension, using a particular weight system, over a specific field. A graph is then classified as degenerate if the corresponding group is degenerate in the context of the group-theoretic framework. Every graph is found to be degenerate except for complete graphs. This degeneration framework is utilized to establish an ordering between graphs, which are all ranked based on their degeneration levels. A particular graph is then classified as 'better' if its degeneration level is lower, and 'worse' if it's higher. It's found that monohomogeneous graphs hold the highest rank, followed by bipermisible graphs, and it's proven that there are 16 different degeneration levels. The study also finds that each of the 16 levels possesses a unique graph, and determines the smallest possible size for these graphs. Furthermore, the research reveals that some of the degeneration levels can be determined through the intersection of two particular graphs, and that some graphs activate a specific degeneration

Recent breakthroughs in AdS/CFT correspondence research, specifically in low-dimensional settings, are explored, concentrating on AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ and AdS$_2$/CFT$_1$ dualities within massive Type IIA string theory. We first examine the solutions derived in 1908.09851 of AdS$_3$ supergravity, coupled with supersymmetry $\mathcal{N}=(0,4)$. These 2d CFT duals are re-evaluated, in conjunction with surface defect representations in D4-D8 bound state-based 5d fixed-point theories. Next, the solutions derived in 2011.13932 with supersymmetry $\mathcal{N}=4$, specifically AdS$_2$ supergravity, are considered in tandem with the dualized 4d and 5d solutions from massive Type IIA string theory. We hypothesize the realization of the time-dependent Coulomb phase in the 2d superconformal gauge theory as an electrically charged AdS$_2$ wave function. We also propose that the 4d/5d duals of this theory exhibit (semi-)non-Abelian symmetries through charged solitons. Additionally, the solutions from 2011.13932 with supersymmetry $\mathcal{N}=8$ may correspond to a chiral algebra candidate for 5d fixed-point theories based on D4-D8 bound state,

In numerous kernelised machine learning tasks, selecting an optimal kernel is a daunting challenge. A new, two-layer kernel network architecture for Gaussian Process kernels offers a solution by formulating the kernel as the product of two mathematical expressions. These expressions are then optimised simultaneously, allowing the kernel to adapt to the data distribution in an intricate way. As the optimisation process unfolds, the intermediate results can be used as hidden features in a subsequent kernel learning step. Empirical evaluations on benchmark datasets reveal that this kernel architecture, referred to as a double neural kernel within a Gaussian Process, consistently yields high accuracy and delves deeper into the underlying data compared to conventional kernels. It is also notable for its robustness against overfitting, and the intermediate features it produces can be utilised as a means to visualise the essential patterns in datasets. Moreover, the results show that these features can be explained using uncomplicated mathematical expressions such as $1/(1+e^x)$, that is, the sigmoid function, which affirms the theoretical predictions and reduces the complexity of interpreting the models. Finally, the code for this research has been made available for free.

Future high-energy muon colliders face a challenge due to in-flight decays of
muons from the beam line, resulting in beam-induced backgrounds (BIB). This
background interference will hinder accurate data analysis and detector
operation unless mitigated. Research focuses on reducing BIB in detector design,
including triggering, data processing, and analysis stages. Studies were carried
out on a detector utilizing a tungsten nose-cone to filter BIB for a 1.5 TeV
energy threshold. In-depth analysis targeted the innermost detector sections with
highest densities, while conceptual design proposals aimed to optimize a
calorimeter for efficient BIB suppression.

Introducing Spartan, a novel approach for training neural networks with pre-defined sparsity. This method effectively leverages a combination of two techniques: soft parameter pruning through optimal transportation and hard parameter sparsification during forward passes. This dynamic balance enables initial exploration of various sparsity patterns and gradually shifts towards optimizing parameters with respect to a predetermined sparsity pattern. Spartan offers flexibility in incorporating diverse sparsity policies, encompassing both random and structured sparsity, as well as cost-sensitive allocation guided by per-parameter models. Spartan demonstrates exceptional performance on ImageNet-1K classification, achieving significant sparsity in ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16 models while maintaining accuracy within 1% of their fully dense counterparts.

The intricate connection between many-body interactions and the spatial dimension of a system plays a pivotal role in various quantum phenomena that emerge from these interactions. Although the product of maybody interaction and spatial dimension is relatively constant, factors such as spin and charge properties can alter this interaction's nature, giving rise to a diverse range of quantum effects like universal critical behaviors, quasiparticle lifetimes, and thermal characteristics. In a study focused on a spinless Bose gas in one dimension, researchers explore the relationship between many-body interaction and spatial dimension by examining the system's thermal characteristics using a perturbative approach based on the non-relativistic S-matrix theory. They discovered that the product of maybody interaction and spatial dimension influences the coefficient of heat capacity in one-dimensional Bose gas. Furthermore, through an analysis of known and simulated thermal characteristics, researchers found that the product of maybody interaction and spatial dimension can serve as a measure of spatial dimension in systems where repulsive and attractive interactions are present. This conclusion was validated in a scenario where the product of maybody interaction and spatial dimension approaches a constant value from both the repulsive and attractive perspectives. The study also offers a method to calculate thermal characteristics in various types of systems with strong or weak interactions.

Software developers widely acknowledge the importance of unit testing as a crucial aspect of their work cycle, allowing for swift detection and resolution of coding errors. However, test code can be compromised by suboptimal design or implementation choices referred to as test smells. These shortcomings can significantly undermine the quality of software systems by increasing the difficulty of maintenance, aggravating bugs, and hindering refactoring efforts. Although several studies have investigated the potential impact of test smells on test code, they have not yet extensively examined how developers subjectively assess and deal with these issues. This research aims to bridge that gap by asking developers to evaluate test smells in an online survey, thus shedding new light on how developers subjectively perceive test smells. The findings indicate that developers subjectively agree on some test smells' negative effects but disagree on others. Furthermore, possible reasons for these agreements and disagreements are discussed, and a set of recommendations for future research is proposed to explore the practical implications of test smells.

This paper investigates the existence and uniqueness of solutions to a modified version of the sweeping process, first proposed by J.J. Moreau in the early 1970s as part of plasticity theory. The proposed modification involves a novel combination of the prox-regular moving set and two types of perturbations: a Carathéodory mapping and an integral force with an integrand dependent on time variables. To address this new force, a specific class of prox-regular moving sets is developed, allowing for the analysis of forces that vary with time and are only measurable, rather than being continuous or adapted to a filtration. By considering the most general case, this work deviates from prior research, which typically imposed stronger assumptions. To determine movement in the presence of friction and other non-smooth forces, the sweeping process with these modified perturbations represents a significant advancement in the mathematical toolset for plasticity theory and other related fields.

We introduce the updated version of the {\tt KKMCee} event generator, version 5.00.2, designed for simulating lepton and quark pair production through high-energy electron-positron annihilations. As the most advanced generator for this process, the code, now rewritten entirely in modern C++, maintains all features of its Fortran 77 predecessor, while incorporating several enhanced Monte Carlo algorithm improvements. Its capabilities, supplemented with next-to-leading order QED corrections, genuine weak corrections using the {\tt DIZET} library, and polarized $\tau$ decays facilitated by {\tt TAUOLA}, serve as a starting point for future updates to achieve the high precision needed for next-generation lepton colliders. Moreover, this version integrates {\tt HEPMC3}, a new interface that replaces {\tt HepEvt}, to connect the {\tt KKMCee} with other essential components such as parton showers and detector simulations. Specifically, this new interface enables the utilization of {\tt PHOTOS} for additional photon emissions in $\tau$ decays, now rewritten in the C language for improved functionality. Ultimately, this version of the {\tt KKMCee} generator ensures the smooth transition from its predecessor while taking full advantage of modern coding paradigms.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult due to interference from background noise, channel noise, and the effects of EMG interference. This issue becomes more severe in mobile ECG devices where electromagnetic noise is prevalent. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel Tiramisu Model for IBI estimation that outperforms existing methods with higher precision and accuracy while being suitable for embedded systems with limited processing power and resources.

To utilize contemporary computing systems efficiently, an important consideration is reducing the communication cost associated with data transfer, which is especially relevant when working with high-order tensor data types. A recent development in data analysis, tensor singular value decomposition (t-SVD) is a high-order extension of the well-known singular value decomposition (SVD) from matrix analysis. It was previously shown in a pioneering work that subspace randomization can effectively decrease communication costs for t-SVD by reducing the required passes (data transfers) from O(n^d) to approximately d. Building on this concept, our research offers a novel and more general randomized algorithm for t-SVD that is applicable to any number of passes (d ≤ n), is suitable for contemporary computing architectures, and is also adaptable to memory-constrained systems. Moreover, our new method retains the remarkable statistical efficiency and robustness of the original subspace randomization approach.

Network analytics heavily relies on embedding static graphs in low-dimensional vector spaces to enable node classification, link prediction, and visualization, but this approach struggles to accommodate dynamic behavior exhibited by real-world networks. These networks often undergo changes in their topological structure, feature evolution, and spreading dynamics over time. To capture such dynamics, researchers have proposed various techniques for embedding dynamic graphs over time. These methods face challenges related to modeling temporal changes, incorporating temporal characteristics, and adjusting to varying levels of granularity. This overview survey aims to provide a comprehensive summary of dynamic graph embedding by discussing its fundamental aspects and presenting a comrade category to clarify the different embeddings and dimensions. We also review multiple dynamics concepts and model their impact on graphs, examining the existing methods for graph embedding as well as matrix factorization and the most advanced DGE methods in detail. Additionally, this work evaluates and contrasts the various DGE techniques and model various datasets to study their effectiveness. Finally, this research identifies open issues and future avenues for investigation.

Our investigation into a $^7$H resonant ground state involves the $SSD$ partial wave and focuses on determining the seven neutrons' resonance energy. The theoretical framework relies on a $SSD$ Born model, and by calculating the $SSD$ scattering amplitude, we derive the resonant energy at approximately 4.58 MeV above the $^3$H+4n threshold, with a lifetime of around 2.4 ns. This research combines theoretical models with experimental data from direct searches for $^7$H resonances, yielding results that can be compared to those from experimental group searches.

This research paper investigates a Nirenberg type problem on the upper half spheres with the aim of finding conformal metrics that satisfy a prescribed scalar curvature and zero mean curvature on the boundary. The investigation is focused on solving a boundary value problem, denoted as (P), that incorporates the critical Sobolev exponent. The equation (P) involves a nonlinear term with the exponent (n+2)/(n-2) and can be stated as:

$(P)$

$\begin{cases}
   \nabla^2 u -  \frac{n(n-2)}{4}u = Ku^{ \frac{n+2}{n-2}},\ u>0
  in  S^n_+,\\ 
 \frac{\partial u}{\partial \nu}= 0
 on $\partial  S^n_+$.

\end{cases}$ 

A function K, with $K\in C^2(S^n_+)$ and K > 0, appears in the equation. The existence of finite energy solutions is shown for a subcritical approximation of (P) under certain generic conditions on the function K, resulting in the occurrence of multiple solutions. These solutions feature multiple clusters of boundary layers along the vertical axis, whose locations change depending on the position and spatial invariance of the function K, utilizing a new tool named Bubi. Deep Metric Learning methods primarily aim to develop a space where data similarities can be accurately maintained. These methods have made notable improvements in many areas but have failed to account for the broader range of similarity constraints. This oversight has led to suboptimal performance in situations where class data exhibits more complex similarity patterns. The implementation of the widely used Triplet Loss is a case in point. This method learns from data pairs that are akin to nearest neighbors, resulting in a space where nearest neighbors correspond to similar classes. While Triplet Loss performs well in certain scenarios, it is less effective in situations where there are significant differences in data sub-classes. The presence of such complexities has prompted the use of more flexible and deeper models for learning metrics. These models can be trained using minimization techniques that capitalize on specific loss functions, like the Angular Embedding Loss, to be incorporated into the Neural Networks. The measurement tool for optimizing techniques measures the distance between data objects using a complete metric like Cosine, Euclidean, or Gaussian, despite the fact that these metrics might not be the best choices for data. The incorporation of the loss functions is achieved by considering each data object as an embedded object within a reduced-dimensional space. The use of lower-dimensional spaces for data objects enables metric creators to be more precise, as the data objects' distances are a result of nearest neighbor search.
